speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of the statement yesterday by the Premier of Alberta-a statement of policy, as he described it-to the
October 30, 1979

effect that the people of Canada would have to buy oil at a price which Alberta decided to be fair, or not get it from Alberta.
Will the Prime Minister give his assurance to the people of Canada that Canadian oil, whether it be produced in a province or offshore, will continue to be available to Canadians?

subtopic: OIL PRICES-AVAILABILITY OF CANADIAN OIL TO CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Prime Minister would care to elaborate on his own policy and assure the House that he has the means to carry out that assurance. The Prime Minister will recall that last Wednesday, in this House, he said he would not under any circumstances use the declaratory power or emergency power.
How can he give the assurance to Canadians that they will get a continuous supply of Canadian oil, in circumstances such as the Premier of Alberta described? What power would the Prime Minister use under the constitution, or would he invoke the Petroleum Administration Act?

subtopic: OIL PRICES-AVAILABILITY OF CANADIAN OIL TO CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has cited two options that are open to the Government of Canada in the event of that kind of emergency. 1 say to him, and 1 assure the House and the country, that I do not think we are facing that kind of emergency. 1 do not intend to react to a proposal that might have been made but certainly has not yet been made to me.
I do not think we are yet at a stage in this country where oil pricing matters are going to be resolved by long-distance accusations. I remain confident that we can work out an agreement involving the federal government and the various provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one aspect of the oil question is, of course, the matter of supply. The other aspect, one which has deeply concerned both Americans and Canadians, is the question of profiteering in the industry.
Considering that in the United States the President has responded swiftly and imaginatively by proposing a $300 billion excess profits tax on multinational oil companies in the United States, I should like to ask the Prime Minister, bearing in mind that Imperial Oil, Shell, Texaco and Gulf have reported profit increases in Canada for the first nine months of this year of approximately 55 per cent, for a cumulative total of about, $1 billion in profits, whether he will follow the American lead in dealing with this serious question by immediately establishing in Canada a commission with authority to investigate prices and profit increases in the oil industry and to order roll-backs in prices and profits should such action be justified.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the proposal of the Leader of the New Democratic Party of such an agency was brought to my attention outside the House. One oil company in Canada, Imperial Oil, through proceedings which became clear in a civil court, is on record as having overcharged the consumers of Nova Scotia. It is also on record as having avoided paying federal income taxes by creating a dummy corporation in Bermuda. What, specifically, does the Prime Minister have in mind to deal with these problems, or is he simply content to talk tough to the Canadian people about dealing with inflation but not to act tough at all with multinationals?

speechtext:

It concerns the government's intentions regarding the severe economic disruption and hardship presently being experienced by the soft drink industry as a result of the government's handling of the 1.5 litre container problem.
Recognizing that jobs have been jeopardized, and that indeed in New Brunswick, in the community of Woodstock, 32 employees have been laid off, I would ask: Can the Prime Minister report on the progress being made toward finding a solution to the problem of glass retention from 1.5 litre containers? Has the government taken measures to protect the confidentiality of information filed in government computer banks and, if so, in what way?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speechtext:
After introducing its electronic data processing (EDP) policy in 1972, Treasury Board subsequently issued directives to departments on computer security matters in 1974. At the same time a Security Evaluation and Inspection Team (SEIT) was created within the RCMP to review security measures in computer installations, including private sector service bureaux handling government information.
Departments report back to the RCMP on the implementation of SEIT recommendations. The RCMP reports annually to the Treasury Board Secretariat on the state of computer security in government. Computer security standards are now being developed. For computer work performed on private sector computers, security requirements are part of the contractual arrangements with the supplier. Part IV of the Human Rights Act requires that the use of computer banks containing personal information be strictly controlled, including new uses of existing data.
An area of considerable concern is the linking of computer banks, for instance using SIN numbers to obtain more complete information on individuals. The government is preparing legislation that will ensure greater legal protection against unauthorized disclosure of personal information and put constraints on the ability to link files using SIN, by limiting the number of uses for the SIN number. This legislation will be introduced in this session of Parliament.

The House resumed from Monday, October 29, 1979, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-17, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, like other members on this side in the official opposition 1 was quite content to stay satisfied with the well-crafted Liberal legislation which had been presented by the Conservative party. But after listening last evening to the rather poetic description given to us by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) on Tory economic policy as being similar to someone's exposed backside ascending toward heaven, I was so inspired by that particular description of how Conservatives carry out their economic analysis that I felt it deserved at least some reply from members on this side. I suppose by way of corollary we could say that if that is a description of the way in which the Tories measure their economic performance, we can say the devil takes the hindmost in these circumstances.
Listening to the debate on this particular tax bill demonstrated to me one very clear reason why it is that this country needs a Liberal party. As we listen to the exaggerations from the left and the right, each expressing his or her own form of pristine power theology, it becomes clear that if this country were to be allowed to polarize between the extremes, such as is being advocated by members in this group and that group, what would happen is that the country would become so totally confused and overwhelmed by hyperbole of these orthodoxies

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
that nothing practical or realistic could be done in the way of tax policy.
There is perhaps no more important debate that takes place in this House than the analysis and estimate of how we want to allocate our taxes. It is the basic foundation document of our economic order. It determines very clearly who pays and who gets the benefits in our society. If we were simply to follow the preachments and teachings of those on the left and the right, we would find out we have a society which is carved into two totally discrete, disparate groups in which there is no common ground.
I was interested last night to hear the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) talk about the two teams of tight money.
I tended to agree in part with his analysis. There are two teams in this House. There is also a group of kibitzers on the left, the armchair quarterbacks who will never be in the game. They say they never have the opportunity to make decisions. They can afford to exercise their particular form of virtue. Someone once said you can have a lot of virtue if you have never been subject to temptation. That is certainly the case with the New Democratic Party. Of course they can express themselves with sanctimonious, virtuous statements about how to run the world. However, when have they ever had the opportunity to do anything about it? They are the classic eunuchs. They are very adapt at talking about sex because they never have to participate in it. They are really the grand observers in our economic order. They know they will never have to govern. If they want to be the kibitzers, the armchair quarterbacks observing the scene and offering their soapbox preachments, that is fine with us, but let us get back to serious debate.
Oh, oh!
Order, please. We should extend the hon. member the courtesy of the House to continue his speech. Can we have order.

What happens with soapbox artists, Mr. Speaker, is they are able to produce a lot of noise but no light. That has been their basic practice in this House. As long as they can keep yelling, screaming, pounding and clapping, no one will really bother looking at what they have to say, which usually adds up to nothing anyway.
What should concern members of this House is not so much what is happening with the rump group in the corner, but that many of the same bad habits are being picked up by members opposite. They think in this time and age the only way to combat the purities of the left wing is to ascribe a purity to the right wing.
We had a perfect example in the speeches last night when we were raised to elevations by the theological purity of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) regarding the free market, that wonderful mechanism that has done so much for so long. As a result we have this basis of total domination
[Mr. Axworthy.)
versus the free market. It is beginning to sound as if this is a college common room. We are not talking about practical things any more.
We have the theorists and philosophers on the right now combining with the theorists and philosophers on the left. I am afraid that theology is not what is in order in Canada today. We need hard economics. The only exception to that is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) who does not believe in theology but thinks he is Johnny Carson. He thinks that rather than worry about economic policy, he should practise his new comedy routine.
The question we have to pose is, when do we get serious about the economic conditions of this country? When do we start looking at taxation policies which are going to make some practical sense? If I still have a moment or two, perhaps I can provide some illustrations to these philosophers to the left and the right. I do not want to confuse them with the facts; I know that would interfere with their particular sort of music.
It is important to recognize certain facts about the way the economy has been working in this country. Let us deal with these gentlemen on the right. They seem to feel there is an enormous burden hanging around the necks of the Canadian taxpayer, that everyone is walking around overburdened by this enormous government expenditure. They like to parade in front of us glorious examples, such as a country like West Germany which is so free of these kinds of burdens and whose economy is so forceful.
I wish to point out that according to a recent report by the OECD the percentage of expenditure in Canada of government taxation related to the gross national product is less than in West Germany. How does that fit with the facts that are constantly paraded before us, that the amount of taxation that is dispensed in this country is less than in West Germany? It is only one percentage point above that of the United States, the home of free enterprise. Therefore, this enormous burden we have been told about simply does not exist in terms of the facts.
What does exist is that there is a large cluster of countries, all of which have a percentage between 30 and 35 per cent of their GNP. Obviously that suggests there are more complicated and more real factors at work in the economy than the hyperbolic situation of this enormous government albatross bearing down upon the backs of the people.
The Tories simply do not look at where the economy is going or what it has been doing. They prefer to deal in the areas of vision and fantasy rather than look at the facts. The facts are here in the Department of Finance report. I suggest that the Minister of Finance, who so conveniently provides memoranda for members of the finance committee, should provide some of the same literature from his department to his own caucus and recommend that they start reading these facts.
On the same kind of account, I listened with a great deal of amusement to the hand-wringing, teeth-gnashing and caterwauling of the NDP last night about how for yeaifs those nasty Liberals had really put it to the poor people. That is the kind
October 30, 1979

of sob story we received about how awful the tax system would be.
I refer members of the NDP to the same report, which points out in terms of lower income groups that they have a much higher degree of discretionary income than almost any other country in the OECD. In fact, it has improved by close to 50 per cent in the past three or four years. When you look at the number of tax exemptions that are available to low and modest income Canadians, they have far more tax exemptions than are available to the West Germans, Americans or those in most any other country.
All of a sudden we have found that rather than have the previous government in the back pockets of the big corporations, as they like to testify, the fact is they have far more discretionary income and there have been far more initiatives taken to lower taxation for those groups. As a result, there is far more income available to the very group about which they are concerned.
A member from one of the Vancouver ridings, I forget which one it is, used a term which 1 do not think is considered parliamentary under the Hansard arrangement. 1 would not want to repeat it. I would suggest to her, if that is so, that she take a course in straight reading of English. I am prepared to do that for her. I know it is not printed in the language that she is prepared to use as it does not include those kinds of phrases, but it does suggest that for the income group under $5,000, discretionary income for a family of four has gone up 8.3 per cent over the past year; and for the income group between $5,000 and $10,000 it has gone up 9.4 per cent in the last year. Again, 1 know they do not want to be confused by the facts. I know that is not the socialist way to live. They do not want to look at what is real or effective. They simply want to go by the theories learned at the knee of some U. of T. professor. It is about time they looked at the facts so that their economic comments could be more effective and useful.
Once we get away from the political dialogues coming from left and right we can start looking at the real problems in taxation policy, and there has been no more real problem apparent than the whole issue of what we should do about interest rates, because those rates are directly related to the tax policies we have in place. When we look at the statements being made by members of the government the first thing we should discount is their constant survival technique of saying "It was your fault." The fact is that many of the measures now being introduced were not the fault of those previous Liberals but are initiatives taken by this government.
I point out one particular concern. We find the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) pledging that they are going to stand in the trenches and fight the good battle against inflation. They are going to be Horatio on the bridge and get tough and do all the things that are required. They say, "Boy, if it's going to hurt the people it's going to have to hurt because eventually we are going to get a solution." And how do they propose to solve this problem? They
Income Tax Act
are going to cut back government spending. They are going to reduce the deficit.
Well, members on this side may be excused if we have the odd note of skepticism in our voice. Frankly, we do not know what to believe from members opposite. We heard during the election campaign that the best thing for the Canadian economy was to have a bigger deficit, a stimulative deficit. Apparently those words have disappeared from their vocabulary because we do not hear about a stimulative deficit any more. But that is exactly what they are intending to do, because while they are reaming the Canadian public by the increasing acceleration of interest rates, they are doing absolutely nothing to control deficit spending.
How can they with any honesty or candour stand up and say they are fighting the good economic fight when day after day they bring proposals before the House which would have the result of increasing spending and deficits? While they are talking about the need to hold firm and reduce government spending they are proposing an outlay of an additional $500 million through their mortgage tax program. Where will they get the money for that? Is it going to be concocted out of thin air or do they intend to cut back other worth-while programs? In fact, what they will do is increase the deficit, which will increase the inflationary pressure.
Along the way, Mr. Speaker, we had that grand report from the task force on PetroCan. What does it advocate? It advocates an additional $2.3 billion deficit. Could there be anything more inflationary than suggesting that the way to solve our economic problems is to add $2.3 billion to the existing $11 billion deficit? This really makes the words of the Minister of Finance turn to ashes in his mouth. How can he tell the finance committee he is fighting the good fight when his colleagues in the government are talking about adding billions of dollars to an already substantial deficit? That goes under the definition of total contradiction. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot be talking and plighting your troth about the need to restrict government spending and then have ministers say that if Petro-Canada were privatized it would be the best thing that could possibly happen.
We listened to the hon. member from Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) give us his version of how the economy works; that is something that is probably a cross between Lewis Carroll and Walt Disney in terms of the way in which it develops fancies about the future. He was saying the Tories were going to strengthen Petro-Canada. They would strengthen it first by cutting it in half and turning it over to the private sector, which would be far better managers but would cease to do many of the things that Petro-Canada does, and strengthen it by adding a $2.3 billion deficit to the public treasury. That is a curious way in which to describe the strengthening of this oil agency. It does not add up according to even the simplest economic axiom the Conservatives appear to be using.
The fact of the matter is there is a substantial opportunity to strengthen PetroCan if the government only had the courage to take it, and the way the government could acquire that courage would be to tackle the question of oil pricing, which

they keep pushing further and further away from resolution, simply apply a windfall profits tax, and then turn the major proceeds of that tax over to PetroCan so that it could use that money for investment in energy to the benefit of all Canadians. Let us not go through the mental gymnastics in which the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine and the Minister of Finance constantly engage.
Let us talk about an option which makes some sense. Large pools of capital are being pulled out of the economy of this country and allowed to sit fallow in certain large heritage funds. These funds are not being used for investment in major energy projects, major transportation projects or for major agricultural purposes; they are simply being allowed to go unused. We have the paradox of a government which says they are good economic managers when in fact what they are doing is simply delaying the inevitable and allowing themselves to be used by a provincial premier, one who last evening had the audacity to declare his independence, in effect, from any form of common weal in this country. How the Prime Minister can calmly turn the other cheek to the challenge and threat posed by the statement of the premier of Alberta is beyond me. It simply means that the Prime Minister thinks his way of dealing with the provinces, of avoiding a fight by giving away his lunch all the time, will somehow bring about a peaceful solution. 1 have news for the Prime Minister: he has given away his last piece of lunch, he has nothing more to give. All he has done is set up a self-fulfilling prophecy, because these premiers will go after him with all the more ferocity and all the more ambition, knowing he is not prepared to stand up to them.
It is a form of betrayal of the Canadian people that we do not have a Prime Minister who is prepared to stand up to the Premier of Alberta and say: "It is absolutely necessary that on the matter of oil pricing you do not speak just for 8 per cent of the population; someone has to speak for 100 per cent of the population". I am amazed, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister would allow that kind of declaration of economic separatism to be announced and not be prepared to respond with any form of strength or effectiveness. It was one of the sad moments in the history of this country when the Prime Minister once again backed away from living up to his responsibilities.
There are economic answers available; it is just that the government does not want to tackle them. Let us talk for a minute about a favourite topic of the Minister of Finance who has told us he has some choices available to him when it comes to the problem of high interest rates. He said: "1 have to hold firm on monetary policy but I do have the opportunity to make some choices fiscally". What is the choice he has made? He has made only one choice, and that is to introduce the mortgage tax credit program which he thinks will be salvation for all that ails Canadians. He stands up in the House with a great deal of flourish and says: "Think about the 3.8 million households which will get benefits under this program".
What he does not mention are the other 3.8 million households which will get no benefits under the program. Are

they somehow immune from inflation? Will they somehow be able to avoid the problem of high interest rates? What the minister is really saying is that he only cares about 30 per cent or 40 per cent of the population and that the rest of the population can be forgotten. But it is quite obvious that they, too, are affected by high interest rates.
It is not just homeowners who are faced with the problem of escalating mortgages. One of the major problems we are facing today is in the rental market. Many of those rental units were introduced under the ARP program and carry five-year mortgages at 8 per cent which are coming up for renegotiation. The rate will now be 14 per cent, a 6 per cent increase, and they will either have to declare bankruptcy or suffer substantially ballooned rents far beyond the means of most people living in them. Are they to be forgotten? Is the minister excluding that section of the population which for one reason or another decides to rent rather than own accommodation? Is the Minister of Finance saying he is prepared to forget all those who do not have mortgages and therefore will receive absolutely no benefits whatsoever other than the property tax credit, which this year will be $62.50? Is he forgetting those people who are going to find, as they face increases in oil prices which will add up to $300 or $400 on their housing bills, that somehow they are going to be included in this magic mortgage credit program? Who speaks for them? Where are choices being made for them?
The fact is that what the minister is introducing is bad economic policy. He has himself caught in the campaign commitments of his leader and is now trying to wriggle out by putting as pleasant a face on a bad proposition as he possibly can. However, it is bad economic policy because he has committed major expenditures for this year of $575 million. Next year they will be well over $1 billion and ultimately closer to $3 billion over the long term, when he has no ability, according to his own confession, to forecast what the economy will be like.
The Minister of Finance is introducing a structural economic change when what we are in desperate need of are shortterm responses to real and immediate problems. I am sure the minister's economic advisers have told him that he cannot introduce an economic instrument which has a four-year fixed term to it when the economy is gyrating like a crazy top, partly because of the decisions taken by the Bank of Canada, which is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance. The minister is creating a problem and avoiding solutions.
Solutions are obvious and available to him. He could be taking that $575 million and using it to deal with some of the immediate consequences of those 14.5 per cent and 14.75 per cent interest rates on mortgages and prime loans. For example, he could be providing some emergency assistance for those who have to renegotiate their mortgages. He is condemning thousands of Canadians right now because he is not prepared, as I understand it, to make directives to the banks or the lending institutions. Thus these Canadians are locking them-
October 30, 1979

What I want to speak about this afternoon is the question of tax write-offs on pollution controls. I now come to what I intended to say before I was provoked by the inadequacy of the arguments being advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. I want to speak to the provisions which we find in this bill for tax write-offs on pollution controls. My concern is that this method of seeking to control pollution is woefully inadequate, for a number of reasons on which I should like to elaborate at this time.
First, the amount of money involved, even if this were the right way to go about controlling pollution, is so small as to suggest that this government is hardly serious about pollution control. It hardly represents a massive effort and is revealing in that it appears that this government is not willing to have the corporate sector bear even the cost of a token effort to control pollution. The toughness and the tough decisions that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) likes to talk about as being so characteristic of his government are reserved for the Canadian people alone, with weakness being the characteristic of the government on all other fronts.

Second, this way of seeking pollution control is really not a method of control at all. It leaves the responsibility for pollution control with the companies involved. The problem with this is that these companies have no incentive to use their control mechanisms responsibly once they are in place, or indeed if they are put in place. Neither has the private sector, I submit, an honourable record in this area of concern. Its ability to take initiative and responsibility in this area is not one that inspires confidence, in me at least.
Furthermore, this country has too often been held to ransom by corporations which have threatened to shut down their operations rather than comply with environmental standards. What this provision for write-offs means is a further capitulation to this kind of blackmail, capitulation which establishes once again the principle by which this government lives, and by which indeed the former government lived, and that is the principle of the people of Canada being made to bear the social costs, and in this case the environmental costs, of economic development while the profits from such activities are left to the disposal of private interests.
Third, and following from this observation about social and environmental costs and their relationship or lack of it to private profits, the provision for write-offs is wrong in that it acts as if the corporate sector were too improvished to afford pollution control, and must therefore be the object of government handouts. In addition to the fact that this is another case of handouts that this government does not mind, as opposed to all those other handouts to people who are really in need, which they do mind, it is also a case of corporations being rewarded for not instituting pollution control on their own by government money to do what they should have done in the first place. Hon. members opposite are the people who talk about the true cost of things, about realistic accounting. Yet every attempt to have comprehensive pollution control integrated into the cost of things is resisted. Why is that? Because the market might adjust itself in such a way that they would have to lower the percentage of profits which results from these activities.
I submit that in the absence of public ownership, where cost and profits are born by the same body, that is to say the public, environmental goals and standards should be figured into the real cost of products and ways should be found to do this. Companies should be required to meet these goals and standards out of profits, unless, of course, that is completely impossible and there is a pressing environmental danger.
Mr. Speaker, questions of the environment are too important to be dealt with by measures designed to rely on voluntary actions which absolve governments of responsibility. There is the responsibility of the government to protect the environment, because by doing so it lives up to its undisputed responsibility to protect the people of this country, and living up to this responsibility will mean more than a few tax write-offs.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), in discussing Bill C-17, has taken the position that his party has theology and ideas to offer, but that we Liberals are

very pragmatic. 1 am certainly not ashamed of pragmatism. In fact, I think it is one of the hallmarks of Liberalism. I would also like to say that we too have a number of, not necessarily philosophical ideas, but certainly theoretical ideas which a debate on a bill of this kind gives us the opportunity of putting forth.
Unfortunately it is not providence, I do not think, which permits me to follow the last speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, or the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) who spoke on this bill last night. In fact, it was the whip. Nevertheless, 1 have a number of points which 1 should like to clarify in terms of the presentation made by those gentlemen, particularly the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood.
During the debate last Thursday night, I raised some question with respect to the entire area of the taxation of corporations. The bill with which we are concerned here also touches in a very important way upon corporate tax, particularly with respect to the small business deduction of those corporations which people commonly refer to as professional corporations or service corporations. My concern for this area of corporate taxation goes back many years. This is a philosophical or theoretical argument. The other night I made the point that one cannot tax a corporation. I recall having said that one cannot tax a corporation any more than one can tax a dog, much to the snickering of some members around me. Subsequently a number of people raised the issue with me. Certainly we have a corporate tax, but also there is a dog tax in many municipalities of the country. My point is that a corporation is not a person. A corporation cannot consume goods or services. A corporation is simply a legal fiction which I recall from my studies in law school was defined as existing only in contemplation of the law.
This is very significant in terms of this bill and in terms of the entire area of corporate taxation, because a corporation cannot in fact pay tax. The only people associated with a corporation which can pay tax are the shareholders who must suffer a diminution of their return on investment, or the persons who deal with the corporation, namely, those who buy goods and services from the corporation and to whom the tax inevitably must be passed on. Of course, a corporation is a vehicle for the collection of taxes, as is a trust or a partnership. There is no question about that.
As I pointed out during my comments the other night, the Carter commission fully endorsed that particular concept of taxation. That is why it recommended a full and complete integration of corporate taxation with the taxation of shareholders. In typical fashion we have not gone far enough. We have partial integration. We have a dividend tax credit, but we have never really come to grips with the problem of corporate taxation. We have never recognized sufficiently in our law the economic reality that there is no economic activity in the declaration of a dividend from a corporation to its shareholders.

That brings me to another point raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. I see he is not in his seat; he has joined the ranks of the members across the way. Perhaps the collecting mechanism is not appropriate. If one were to look at the shareholder list of any major bank, one would find a very substantial representation of pension funds and pension trusts of syndicates and of other people, the workers in the country and even people in the constituency of the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. It is completely unfair, and in fact misleading, to look at a bank and say that the bank is paying only 10.7 per cent. The bank is paying nothing in either case. It is the shareholders who are paying. That is the central theme of my comments this afternoon.
Also the hon. member attacked the question of preferred share financing which would include income debenture financing. This legislation is designed to change or basically terminate in many respects that kind of financing. The history of that financing is not all black. The hon. member said that many large corporations have benefited from this financing. The corporation did not benefit from that financing. The shareholders of that corporation benefited and the employees of that corporation benefited, as well as the people who bought goods and services from the corporation. I dare say that a large number of businesses might not even exist in the form they do today had it not been for the availability of that financing. It is the problem of trying to personify the corporation as if it were a person, which it is not.
Pursuing this question somewhat further, I should like to point out that the corporation tax system in the country has had the effect of destroying, or at least not creating or sustaining, tax neutrality. The members on my left and those across the floor can sit here and debate whether rates are appropriate, whether one group or class of people should be paying more or less tax. I am quite prepared to enter into that kind of debate. But what I am concerned about is that which is part of our law today, that which has been institutionalized for many years. I am referring to the fact that the very existence of corporations and their treatment as taxpayers has meant that people in the same financial circumstances are not paying the same amount of taxes.
I am disappointed with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cros-bie). Perhaps he will attack this problem in his November budget; we have not seen it yet. But he has not addressed himself to this problem in an attempt to iron out some of the fundamental inequities which exist.

My point is that the entire area of corporate tax law must be rationalized in some sensible manner. We must look to full integration of corporate and individual taxes. It is long overdue.

The United States has taken initiatives in this regard, as you may know, Mr. Speaker. The result has been, I am advised, that tax shelters, the kind of deals that so many people like to indulge in, both in the United States and in Canada, and the incentive to engage in those kind of transactions is removed. The result, if one were to do a study on it, which has not been the case in this country, would be that the over-all net revenues of government would probably increase. Since the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood has raised this question in respect of doctors, I would suggest that one would see no necessity for these service corporations and a host of other vehicles, be they MURBs, be they films, be they oil wells or be they other things, about which basically I have some reservation in terms of being used to stimulate development in this country. Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the hon. member in view of his definition as to who pays corporate income taxes. He put the argument that it was the shareholder who paid the income tax. Later on in discussing other activities of corporations he indicated that the customers of the services provided by the corporation also paid a share of that income tax because they are the persons who provide the revenue by purchasing the services of that corporation. Would the hon. member not say that a corporation can be looked upon as a mechanism for flowing through funds to a variety of purposes, to the shareholders, to the tax collector, to the employees, etc., but that the burden for paying income tax falls upon all the people who seek sustenance from the corporation and not just the shareholders?

Let me answer that question. I thought I had made that point. The hon. member is quite right, the shareholders pay the tax and the persons who receive goods and services from the corporation pay it. If a tax is levied on a corporation, even if it is 98 per cent, and the return on the investment of the shareholder does not decline, then it is clear that the only people paying at that point are basically the people who receive the goods and services from the corporation. That is another reason why some of these unduly onerous rates of tax have created what is called "tax-push inflation". No matter how much you apply these taxes to one vehicle, as long as that vehicle is capable of passing them on-perhaps I should not use the term "vehicle" as I am starting to personify the corporation. The fact is those taxes are passed on, and that can result in tax-push inflation just as increased wage demands can result in increased inflation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity of making a few brief remarks on the present bill before the House today. I should like first of all to deal with two small aspects of the legislation that relate to the fairness of this tax system and the amendments being proposed, and as well to take a look at some of the aspects of taxation as a tool to shape and strengthen the Canadian economy.
Let me suggest at the outset that the present bill is in no way fair. In the second instance, it does not present any coherent plan to strengthen the Canadian economy.
There are some aspects of the bill that can be supported. We might quibble with the mechanisms that are used, but certainly the expansion of research and development is a very desirable goal within the Canadian economy, as is the development of pollution controls. We have had many days of discussion about the acid rain problem in this country, and it is imperative that we begin to take action on it.
The other thing that will be of particular assistance in rural ridings like mine is the employee expense deduction. There are a few aspects of this bill that can be supported and that will provide constructive help to Canadians, but by and large this is an ad hoc approach to solving a lot of the problems in this country. In some cases the amendments are counterproductive; they are not fair and they do not represent a constructive way

of dealing with many of the economic problems that face our nation.
On the subject of fairness, the first thing I should like to examine is the business of shifting the tax burden from corporate taxation to personal taxation. I noticed with interest the remarks of the previous speaker on this fiction, but nevertheless the business of a corporation exists. They earn income and in some cases, as with foreign corporations, they export a tremendous amount of income from this country. What has occurred over the years is a rising burden of tax on low and middle income taxpayers. This is to the benefit of many of the corporations in this country.
The bulk of this legislation and its amendments is concerned with providing tax savings for corporations in the hope that they will achieve in some way the goals desired by most Canadians. This is extremely unfair. Taxation has to be seen to be fair; otherwise the credibility of the government will be eroded.
I think the Conservative party realized that prior to the last general election when they suggested that they would be prepared to introduce a $2.2 billion personal tax cut. That particular suggestion would have made for a much fairer tax system in the sense that it would have reduced the burden of tax on personal income and started to bring it in line with lightened load on corporate taxpayers.
As we examine this bill, Mr. Speaker, we see a number of provisions designed specifically to relieve the burden of taxation on corporations. These tax savings for corporations will mean higher rates of tax on personal incomes. The first of these, the investment tax credit, will probably not create jobs in this country, and I think this has been mentioned before in this House. We are probably going to see investments made on the basis of long-term profitability and market conditions. The prospect of having an investment tax credit in a very indefinite form means that it will probably wind up as a side benefit to the original decisions on investment.
There is an aspect of this business of investment tax credits and, generally, tax savings that accrue through investment that affects people in my riding and many others along the coast of British Columbia, as well as other areas of the country. This is the situation where a corporation can realize a tax saving by making an investment, usually in technological improvements which result in unemployment. There are examples on the B.C. coast of three major corporations-not small businesses that are usually the single industry in a community where, through technological improvements paid for by tax savings, in the neighbourhood of 750 or 1,000 jobs will be removed. This is the long-term projection. So we have paid with our tax dollars for investments that created unemployment. Not only that, but they remove disposable income from small communities and, indeed, destabilize a very delicate local community economy, which in turn has had some drastic impacts on small business.
Another proposal for tax savings is the blanket approach to providing tax credits for research and development. Certainly
[Mr. Skelly.)
this is a desirable goal within the context of the Canadian economy where research and development is being rationalized by taking it out of the country-a sort of goal of trans-national corporations to centralize research and development.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that perhaps we should begin to consider research and development in terms of providing specific directions within this country. It would be desirable to see an industrial strategy and national economic goals defined for Canada to improve research and development, government joint ventures and other instruments and to encourage this in specific areas that meet our national needs. I am thinking here of things like energy conservation. This is a very critical area and one that we should be moving into.
Another area is the development of transportation. So much of the development of industry and small business in this country depends on effective transportation. Because of the nature of this country we should be leaders in this field.
One aspect of transportation that the government has embraced is marine shipping. There will be a proposal, we hope, for the creation of a deep sea fleet. We have put forward the suggestion that Canadian resources in the Arctic should be transported by Canadian shipping. There is a proposal for the acquisition of naval ships and icebreakers. It is to be hoped that these initiatives can be undertaken in Canadian shipyards. Tremendous amounts of research and development in these areas will be needed if we are to remain competitive with the rest of the world.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to provide tax credits for research and development, these should meet our national goals through a very clearly stated industrial strategy. Such a strategy has not appeared as yet.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) spoke about pollution control equipment. This is a very serious matter in my riding as it is in many others. Unfortunately, as far as taxes are concerned, there is only another blanket proposal respecting pollution control equipment.
I am joined by others in asking why corporations which are earning large incomes, especially foreign corporations, are allowed to deduct the cost of pollution control as a cost of doing business. Why is that being paid for out of the public purse? We should be providing tax benefits to those corporations that must be improved and that have a base of necessity in local communities, but we should also look carefully at the substantial tax savings available to profitable corporations. We should demand a reduction in the cost to the public purse and see to it that those corporations share or shoulder the cost of pollution control.

We have heard a great deal in this House about how oil companies today are receiving windfall profits, how they are manipulating prices to their benefit and how they are seeking tax savings outside this country. The second aspect of fairness deals with a problem that was also brought up last week. Statistics Canada suggested-and this is fairly clear from the evidence that has been gathered and supported over the years-that the gap in income between the top income earners in this country and the bottom income earners is growing. In fact the rich are getting richer and the poor are getting poorer. That is undeniable.
One of the things creating that situation is our tax system. The mechanisms proposed in this bill to attack certain problems are further widening the gap. About 20 years ago the Carter commission enunciated a number of proposals to form the foundation of a fair tax system. The first proposal was "a buck is a buck" and it ought to be taxed. The second proposal was that the income tax system should be progressive.
In the legislation submitted for consideration today and during this week, there are principles opposed to those two ideas. The benefits of tax avoidance such as registered retirement savings plans, incorporation of professional practices and reorganizing the timing of business costs for tax purposes accrue principally to upper income Canadians. Most middle and lower income Canadians do not have enough disposable income to take advantage of the tax savings within those systems, so relief and benefit is provided for the top groups. The principle has been reversed to the point that the income tax system is becoming regressive. Not only do we extract a very high level of tax from middle and low income earners in Canada, but also the business of direct regressive taxation through land tax, through sales and excise taxes and such things, cannot be passed on as a business expense or through tax avoidance. Low and middle income Canadians have to take up these burdens as well. Thus we are placing a very heavy burden of taxation squarely on low and middle income Canadians. The desirable goal would be to move and shift it more fairly on the income range to re-establish the progressive nature of the tax.
For a few moments 1 would like to examine the tax system within the context of a tool to strengthen and shape our national economy and develop an industrial strategy. Unfortunately, our tax system has fostered tax savings which have allowed companies to come here, develop our resources and export those resources for processing in other countries. The maximum advantage from that tax saving has been obtained by those countries and earnings within this country have also flowed out.
Income Tax Act
The major problems in terms of shaping the economy in this country which were defined before the election were unemployment and the lack of an industrial strategy, which saw Canada more heavily dependent upon the development of natural resources and export for processing outside the country. This led to other problems such as the devaluation of the dollar and rising inflation.
The present income tax amendments that we are being asked to consider do not in any way look seriously at using that tax system as a tool to shape and strengthen our economy. We are clearly too heavily dependent on taxation. We have given up other financial instruments in favour of taxation in an effort to control our economy. Taxation appears to be too imprecise in achieving our goals and too cumbersome and imperfect a system to realize them. It weighs very heavily upon middle and low income tax groups.
What we need is co-ordination of economic policy. We need a policy which sees a fair redistribution of the burden of taxation among all sectors of the economy and a restatement or a bringing forward of progressiveness in the tax system. I would suggest that many of the programs which have been developed in this House are unco-ordinated. We see tax proposals that we hope will create jobs and give some direction to investment in this country to strengthen the economy, remove the weakness of the dollar and control inflation. Yet we put one tax program in place and then allow interest rates to rise to the point where investment is discouraged.
Over the last few weeks I have had a number of phone calls from businessmen in my riding. These people would like to take advantage of the proposals which the government has put forward in tax savings, but they have had to forgo making investments because interest rates have put financing beyond their reach. A fellow phoned, most concerned, and mentioned that his project which would have hired 60 people could not now be put forward because of the cost of financing. What we find is that in attempting to achieve one benefit through the tax system, we are destroying it by other manoeuvres in the economy.
I suggest that when that tax bill is put forward-or other manoeuvres in this House-it should be put forward within a context of a very clear industrial strategy in this country, and with it a sense of direction of where we are going. That is something we lost with the previous government. I believe that is what this government was elected to do-to give us a sense of direction and put forward co-ordinated policies that will tell us where we are going.
To summarize, I suggest three things. First, that this bill be examined in terms of fairness. Is a fair burden being placed on the lower and middle income taxpayers by providing tax savings for the corporate sector without a clear statement of what those tax savings are designed to achieve? Second, a complete reduction in the tax system aimed at other fiscal instruments, such as the Bank Act, controlling energy and various other things within the country. Third, we need from the government a clear statement of where we are going in

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
terms of shaping and strengthening the economy for the next generation.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this bill go without saying a few words.
Or any other bill.
Say it again, you will say the same thing.

Perhaps I can say it a few more times at the committee stage, Mr. Speaker.
What we are doing today is debating some old Liberal leftovers which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) is dragging up before the House. These are part of the leftovers he wants the House to swallow. 1 do not think we should be swallowing some of these leftovers quite as quickly as the Minister of Finance wants us to do. A debate on income tax measures gives us a chance to ask the question: What kind of a country do we really want and in which direction do we want to go?
Earlier in the House today we received a sermon from the member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine-1 believe that was the members' riding-
It was Winnipeg-Fort Garry.

The hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I am sorry, 1 get them mixed up. They are sometimes similar in their political ideology. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says, there is not too much difference. Anyway, he was complaining there was a bit too much ideology in the House coming from this side. One of the complaints I have had as an MP since coming here in 1968 is that we have not had enough ideology, we have not had enough sense of direction or enough leadership in this country. I think this country is looking for some courageous leadership.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has been talking about making some tough decisions. About the only thing that 1 have seen that is tough coming from the government so far is that Tory times are tough times for ordinary, little people. We do not need that kind of direction, Mr. Speaker. 1 would like to see the government redistribute income and wealth in this country so that the ordinary citizen-the ordinary Joe, and no pun intended-will get a greater share of the national wealth and pie.
It is about time we did that, yet the bill before us is confirming a lot of the old Liberal diet which was fed to the oil companies. A couple of minor changes were made to give high income people a bigger tax break. 1 ask when will this government live up to its promise of giving a major tax break to ordinary citizens? I can look at a speech made by the Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition during the throne speech debate a year ago and was proposing a major tax cut for low income Canadians. He campaigned on that during the election. In my riding I recall my opponents saying that the ordinary people of this country deserve a tax break,

and that if the Conservative party was elected it would give them a tax break. Is this government doing another Jerusalem on the tax break for the ordinary citizen? Is it doing another Jerusalem on that tax break just as it has done so many Jerusalems already and turned so many flip-flops in policy?
When these people were in opposition they used to scream, bitch and holler in this House that the government was not respecting the rights of Parliament. Yet across the way we had a government in power for five months before Parliament was recalled. Across the way we have a government that has such a lack of respect for Parliament that one of its most powerful cabinet ministers is sitting in the other place, a man defeated by the voters of Ottawa Centre and who was rewarded by being given a senior cabinet portfolio to sit in the other place.
Is this the respect the Conservative policy has propounded? Is this the message we get from the Conservative party? Can we trust that party across the way? I ask these questions because I think this country needs new leadership. This country is crying out for new leadership, as are many parts of the world. There is a real vacuum in the society in which we live. It is not just ironic that the programs watched today by children are "Superman", "Batman", the "Bionic Woman" and the "Six Million Dollar Man". People strive to attach themselves to something "super", something to take away their problems.
The Canadian people have a new government that has promised many things. We do not ask the Prime Minister to be a superman. All we ask is for him to live up to his promises. One of those promises was a major tax cut for the ordinary Canadian citizen. When can we expect that tax cut, or is the Minister of Finance going to have another Jerusalem? Is he changing his mind? I see the Minister of Finance smiling with his big Cheshire cat smile. Perhaps he will reveal something when he gets to his feet in a few minutes' time.
Right on.

When discussing the tax system, it is important to realize that it can be used to make a fair and equitable society. As I said before, we are criticized by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry for being ideological, theoretical or perhaps too dogmatic in our arguments. However, this is a democratic socialist party that believes we have to share the wealth and resources of this country.
We need more equity in this country so that every person, regardless of his background or economic status, is a more equal recipient of the fruits that Canada has to bear. One way of achieving this is to get rid of many of the loopholes and to implement many of the recommendations in the Carter commission report of many years ago, long before a lot of us were in the House of Commons. I refer to write-offs for large companies, write-offs for the business community, entertainment expenses, fringe benefits and privileges given to the wealthy of this country, and deferred taxes for large corporations and companies.
October 30, 1979

When is this new government going to end some of these privileges? They are not rights but privileges. When will these be ended and the money redistributed so the ordinary Canadian citizen can get a real tax break? By the time the high interest rate policy or, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) called it, the tight money policy, gets finished with the economy, those few middle income Canadians who can now afford to buy a home will not be able to do so. The few ordinary income Canadians who are living quite easily will not live so easily with the economic constraints being imposed by this government, be it high interest rates, world energy prices or any of what the Conservative party is introducing to this country.
As 1 said, Tory times are tough times. We should not forget that. I remember my grandfather talking about the days of R. B. Bennett and the old Bennett buggy on the prairies. That was not "Grandfather Knowles" but a different grandfather.
I remember those days very well. That's why I'm here.

When a person could not afford to drive his car, he would take out the motor and hitch the car to a horse. Those were the tough days of the Tory party. The Tory times were tough times. We are getting a bit of that now at the end of the seventies and it will continue into the eighties.
I ask the Minister of Finance not to forget the commitment of the Conservative party to give a significant tax break to ordinary and low income people in this country. 1 ask him to use the taxation system as a tool, a method to redistribute income and wealth in this country so that the ordinary people can harvest a much greater proportion of the national economic pie.

Mr. Speaker, while we do have an opportunity to pose questions in the question period and there are means of parliamentary procedure in this House, this is my first opportunity to speak on this particular bill. I am going to touch on a few points with respect to this bill of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) to borrow $7 billion.
No, no, that's past. This is a different debate. This is the income tax bill.
Income tax. I guess what 1 wanted to comment on on the other bill was the attitude and performance of the minister when he introduced that bill.
That is old stuff. I am changed now!
Are you changed? Is that a change of shirt you are wearing? Is that the new look?
Yes, this is the new me.

Is that the new look for the minister? He has the Bay Street look with his Bay Street shirt. He has been swallowed up by the wolves of Bay Street. The minister has shed his old skin and the positions he took when he sat on this
Income Tax Act
side of the House. He has also shed the positions he held when he was minister of finance under the hon. Mr. Smallwood of Newfoundland.
It is always a very interesting exercise to look at the history of Parliament and what has been stated previously by members in this House. In this case I am speaking particularly of the Minister of Finance and some of the things he said when dealing with the linerboard problem in his province and the millions of dollars that went down the drain as a result of that project. An article was written not too long ago by former premier Smallwood about the mishandling of that project and the role played by this minister. Now he sits here acting as though he has all the magical answers. He comes in here and says he wants to borrow $7 billion.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member is speaking to the wrong debate. He is one week behind in his debate, as usual.

Mr. Speaker, I want to put on the record this afternoon the denial by the Progressive Conservative Party of my motion the other day with regard to income tax. I asked them if they had any charity left in their hearts. I think of the other member from St. John's, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath), who stood on this side and begged, pleaded with and berated the government of the day. He talked about the insensitivity of the government and their lack of compassion and concern for the people of Atlantic Canada.
During this afternoon's question period the Minister of Finance said Treasury Board will not give them the money needed with regard to small craft harbours. All of a sudden there is a complete about face with regard to their concern for the citizens of Atlantic Canada. Now that they are in a position of responsibility and have the power and the ability to make changes, they do not make changes. Why not? What are they waiting for?
Speak to the bill.

I come back to the income tax proposal with regard to galloping inflation, the high cost of living and no control over food prices, with no relief to the consumer in the supermarkets of this country. I am speaking specifically of people on fixed incomes. In my motion under Standing Order 43 the other day, I asked the government to give some consideration to these people on fixed incomes who are hit the hardest. They have no relief, they have no way of overcoming the dire straits they are left in by this government with the fooling about we have witnessed with respect to the price of oil-they won't come clean and tell the people what they are doing. The minister of energy says he is waiting to see what is going to happen with the Premier of Alberta. Now we know why the Premier of Alberta is called the blue-eyed Arab; he says he will dictate to Canadians what we will have to suffer in the months to come. He will not communicate with the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark).

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
We are told by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) that he is waiting to meet with the Premier of Ontario. When will these Conservatives get together? They said it was all going to be rosy once they got into power, that they would all be able to have friendly discussions and friendly negotiations and that we would all be able to see progress. Where is it?
I come back to these innocent Canadians who are caught in the bind of being left to cope with fixed incomes and galloping inflation. This insensitive government will not even give consideration to requests that persons who are over the age of 65 should not be called upon to pay income tax if their income is below a certain fixed amount-the suggestion was $15,000 a year. If you like, maybe we would reduce it to $ 12,000, $ 1,000 a month for persons at the age of 65 with no other income, no other means of support, who are living at what would be considered today, with the cost of rent, food and fuel being so high, to be at the poverty level or below. The government could at least address itself to the needs of people in this sector and give them some consideration.
The minister became excited when 1 referred to how proud he was of introducing his bill to borrow $7 billion. When I referred to that a moment ago, his attitude was: No, no, don't talk about that, we want to sweep that under the rug. You know, Mr. Speaker, they used to be concerned when one talked about millions, and now $7 billion means nothing at all to this minister. He says: "Just give us the power, give us the borrowing authority, but don't question it, though. We are going to be an open government, but don't ask us what we are doing while we are doing it, just let us go". Not at all, Mr. Speaker. I do not think the opposition parties are going to allow members over there to get away with it. They are the same people who sat here previously making wonderful suggestions as to how they were going to solve all the economic ills of the country. Well, they have had five or six months and we have not seen much by way of action.
I certainly wanted to take the opportunity on this income tax bill to register my remarks about the performance of the minister the other day. When he presented his bill he used the word "outrageous". I would say his performance was outrageous. I found it totally unacceptable. The tone and the attitude of some of the things he had to say at random on such a serious matter as borrowing $7 billion was such that the word I would use would be the word he used the other day, that is to say, outrageous. It was an outrageous performance for any minister of finance. Everyone in this House wants to have respect for a minister of finance and I would want to continue in that tradition, but when we see his hilarious attitude almost bordering on being a joke, I think we cannot let this type of thing pass without underlining it and making a comment about it.
If the minister wants to be gracious enough to take these remarks in the way they are intended, we may see an improvement in his attitude in introducing bills in the future. I would implore him in the coming weeks and months when he is with his cabinet colleagues, specifically the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie), to take a hard look at taking some action to find ways and means to alleviate the heavy burden on persons in this country who are retired, senior citizens on fixed incomes, who desperately need assistance at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is obvious that as an economy grows it becomes more possible to redistribute income. When an economy within a capitalistic framework or a mixed economy framework or what is called a "command economy" fails to grow, acute problems are developed in redistributing the wealth or income of that nation. So the small "c" and the capital "C" Conservatives in this country are trying to tell us now that before we can get proper redistribution of income the economy must grow. They are thinking largely in terms of the 1960 type of growth; that is, growth of the gross national product, an index which, in our terms and value judgment, is often as much "gross" as it is national product. But in economic terms, although it is a weak form of estimate it is one of the best we have.
One of the great difficulties with a mixed enterprise system controlled by the invisible government of the large multinationals, as we saw once again during the question period today when the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) did so much to defend his friends and the old friends of the Tories and of the Liberals, especially the oil companies-
Same old story!

It is interesting to note that under the guidance of the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), after meeting out in Winnipeg the Liberals decided to reform and go back to what they called their reformed status before the last five, six or seven years when they were copying everything from the NDP. So they have this little man from Windsor West to be the David attacking the Conservative Goliath under the guise not only of the NDP philosophy but of the programs and suggestions my party has put forward down through the years, and in the four years just gone by when that government failed to adopt so much of what we were suggesting. Why? Because they could not get the economy going.
Shame!

We now have a government of so-called Progressive Conservatives who, as my leader has said, are progressive before an election when they are promising tax cuts and so on but become very, very conservative after the election. They are, in fact, regressive conservatives under the leadership of the present Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), who as everyone in the House knows is an honourable gentleman, one to one. But they are absorbed
[Mr. Harquail.1
October 30, 1979

with the idea that they must bring us back to the time equivalent of the thirties.
Mr. Speaker, if it were not for all the things the NDP and the social democracies of the western world have built up in the meantime, God help us now. Even they have to admit that what is keeping the whole system from collapsing now is what has been built up by the party in this corner. Where now are those voices which were raised from Liberal and Tory benches against the children's allowance legislation, calling it a bonus for procreation? Where are those who denounced unemployment insurance on the grounds that it would make us a nation of weaklings and lazy people? This is now re-emphasized by the right-wing Tories who have gotten a grip over the half dozen or so so-called red-necked Tories from the maritimes. They seem to have caved in before the onslaught of the Alberta Tories and some of the other extreme right-wing, doctrinaire free-enterprisers such as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens).
Look at the contradiction. The Minister of Finance defends restraint and says that everybody has to suffer, and so does the Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance protects and favours the wealthy so that self-employed individuals and professionals can have their own corporations and pay a much lower rate of taxation. Using Liberal tactics, this same government comes along and gives the Atlantic region the investment tax credits which are explicit in this bill, knowing darned well that to the small business community of the Atlantic region this means nothing, given the increases in interest rates which have been adopted since the Conservatives were elected.
Mr. Speaker, those increases in interest rates wipe out all advantages. There will be little or no gain. What gain there might be will be marginal as far as development in the Atlantic region is concerned and as far as the manufacturing sector is concerned. We have a situation where the government is protecting high-income professionals as well as the multinational corporations 1 mentioned, which are the invisible government. Let us face it, oil companies in the United States and here, as well as banks, form a link. It is not a conspiracy but there is a definite link between the other place and the large institutions which govern our way of life. Anyone who attacks that type of incestuous relationship, for want of a better term, which has grown and which has been nurtured in this country is considered extreme. If that is so, I am happy to be called an extremist because it is time these powerful institutions were whittled down to size and put in their proper place. We have amendments to this tax bill which is presently in favour of the "well to do."
Getting back to small business and the fisheries sector, it is especially sad to see the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans bow his head and say the government had to slash $10 million from the small crafts and harbours program in order to carry out its restraint program. Where to a large extent is the slashing taking place? It is taking place in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces.
Income Tax Act
Not Newfoundland.

One and a half million dollars was slashed in Newfoundland. That is a very substantial amount for inshore fisheries. In my constituency the former government and an entrepreneur, using vehicles which had been established, succeeded in building three boats at $1 million each. Under an agreement with the fisheries minister there was to be dredging of the Glace Bay harbour this year. We expected changes but within five months they cut moneys allotted for the dredging of that harbor. The government did not consider how a cut would affect small businessmen and processing plants there.
The result was that the boats, which cost $3 million on a shared basis and which could have created jobs in the inshore fishery and in processing, cannot even get into the harbour. There are no funds for dredging harbours, but this government is now prepared to give special tax concessions to professional self-employed people. It will not look after the inshore fishermen of the Atlantic region. There is contradiction and inequity.
Surely to God there must be a majority of hon. members opposite who feel conscience-stricken about this type of thing. We could not get the former government to move in a significant way on a better redistribution of income, but how can the minister not bring forward any changes today after the release just recently by Statistics Canada showing that the number of poor, those spending 62 per cent of their earnings on food, clothing and shelter, has grown? That number has grown substantially.
I would like to quote from a study undertaken by Statistics Canada and released just three weeks ago:
In 1978, the poorest fifth of the population, those families and unattached individuals getting less than $6,288 for the year, received 3.9 per cent of pre-tax income in the economy, up a little from 3.8 per cent in 1977, but well below the 4.2 per cent it received 11 years ago.
The wealthiest 20 per cent, those with annual incomes in excess of $26,792, received 42.5 per cent of pre-tax income last year, up from 42 per cent in both 1977 and 1967.
The Carter Royal Commission on Taxation recommended that the top personal income tax rate be reduced from 90 per cent, including provincial taxes, to 50 per cent so that "economic doers" and "risk-takers" would have an incentive to earn more money. The tax rate was lowered, but some of these "economic doers" and "risk-takers" such as accountants, doctors and lawyers, felt that they needed a further break. They sought to be protected under the old Liberal bill, and now, to show that there is no difference essentially between the Liberals and the Tories, the Minister of Finance backs up what the Liberals wanted to do. We know the contributions these professionals make. Many here belong to the legal profession. There are a number of doctors and others here, but this is a time when we are demanding that people lower their expectations. The government is preaching that day in and day out, just as the former prime minister did. Surely to the Lord the people who should make sacrifices are the professionals and not the ordinary people of Canada. Surely the poor who were

There is essentially no difference between the Liberals and the Tories in this matter. They want to protect large multinational corporations almost exclusively, despite new protests and the so-called reform of the Liberals, which we suspect is not genuine. We saw the Liberals in action here for a long time, and they protected large multinational corporations. The same thing is going on now. Even though the friends of the Prime Minister are in the oil industry, it seems as though he will not be doing enough for them when he dismantles Petro-Canada. Why should he have to give them special protection when the American Congress now has some seven bills before it which are attempting to establish a national oil corporation in the United States? When will there be a government in Canada which says something different?
We now have Tweedle-dee and Tweedle-dum, and there seems to be little difference between them. When they come together collectively, they can always be counted on to protect large corporate interests and certain special interests. As 1 have said before, there has not been a word from this government about people in the Atlantic region and small businesses whom it says it loves so much. By allowing interest rates to rise to the extent they have risen, people in the Atlantic region and in small businesses there are going to suffer greatly. Individual consumers are going to suffer greatly.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext:
Order, please. Without precluding the consideration of the bill which is before hon. members at this time, may I be permitted to bring to the attention of the House the fact that there is a deficiency, to my mind, in the title of this bill. As hon. members know, the bill received first reading on October 24 together with a group of other bills that have been presented at the opening of this parliamentary session, which did not really give sufficient time for the Chair to see whether the bill has met all the requirements. My concern is that the title of the bill should be phrased in such a way as to cover all the provisions in the bill.
Citation 361 in Beauchesne's fourth edition confirms my contention. It reads:
(1) In framing the title care must be taken to make it wide enough to cover all the provisions of the bill,
May 1 also refer hon. members to Erskine May's nineteenth edition at page 465, which refers to long titles. It states:
The long title sets out in general terms the purposes of the bill, and should cover everything in the bill.
Hon. members will notice that the bill before us is meant to amend two different acts. One is the Canadian Human Rights Act and the second is the Public Service Superannuation Act. To my mind the title given by the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) to this bill is deficient in that the bill is presented as a new act.
My suggestion to the House is that Bill C-217 be entitled "an act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act (age of retirement) and to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act". I believe the House should consider giving unanimous consent to this modification of the title, following which hon. members may proceed with the debate of the bill. Is there

consent from the mover of the motion and from hon. members for the suggested modification?
