On Clause 2-

Mr. Chairman, before the party opposite brays this bill through, I wonder if it might be possible to explain to hon. members present in this committee precisely what the purpose of this particular clause is, what its effect is, and what the cost is to the treasury. We have some objection to it. It provides for a partial write-off of certain charges on land which are incurred by developers. I think it would be of interest to the House to have an explanation from the minister on what is in this particular clause, rather than having these things go through without the Canadian public understanding them at all.

Mr. Chairman, Section 10 of the act deals with inventories. Subsection 10(1.1) deals with land included in the inventory, for example, the land of a land developer. This particular subsection provided that interest and property taxes relating to undeveloped land or included as part of the cost of the land held as inventory-such expenses will not be deductible in the year they are incurred. As a part of the cost of the land, interest and property taxes were deducted only in the year in which the land was sold. The budget proposed a change in the treatment of carrying charges on land. After November 16, 1978, such costs are to be deductible on a current basis. This is dealt with in the amendment to subsection 18(2) of the act, in clause 6 of the bill. As a result of that amendment subsection 10(1.1) of the act is no longer required. It is clause 6, however, that really deals with this particular manner.
While we are here, Mr. Chairman, could the minister tell us what this will cost?
About $30 million.

Thirty million. Is the minister saying that that is going to the developers of this country? Is that right?
October 30, 1979
This will be a tax concession to land developers so that they can deduct the carrying charges on their land.
Of $30 million?
It will cost the Canadian government $30 million in the full year. 1 should clarify that, however. It is not that they are going to get something new; they are going to get it quicker.

Mr. Chairman, one of the most important factors in the increased cost of living in the last 10 or more years has been the very dramatic increase in the price of housing and the cost to the ordinary citizen of buying or renting a house. In the cost of housing, the cost of land has gone up substantially more than the cost of the actual house.
If there is one group in this country that has done very well, it is the large land developers. Their profits have increased astronomically. I cannot understand why we are extending their privileges so that they need not pay taxes on money borrowed to buy land which they will not use for three, five or ten years from now. By that time the land will be worth much more than it is now. We are permitting them to do that by allowing them to charge the interest on the money borrowed as a legitimate business expense.
I cannot think of any way better calculated to encourage them to expand their operations so that they can milk the people of Canada more than they have done in the past, than the kind of amendment the minister is proposing. It is just another rip-off in the long list of rip-offs we have permitted to developers in this country.

Mr. Chairman, that is not the case at all. This amendment is in response to the findings of the Greenspan report. I think I mentioned Mr. Greenspan in the House yesterday. He is the Liberal lawyer from Toronto who did a report for a federal-provincial task force studying the land development process in Canada. He is supportive of the mortgage interest and tax credit plan that we have proposed. He had an excellent article on this in the Globe and Mail which I can recommend to hon. gentlemen. He made the finding that this should be done.
If these costs are made currently deductible, they should afford the land development industry an increased cash flow and give them the opportunity to plan and carry out more projects in Canada.
If hon. members of the NDP are interested in getting more housing, getting land developed and having Canadians housed at an economic cost, this is an amendment that they will support. It is not a rip-off, nor any of the things they have described. It is assistance to the land development industry to improve their cash flow. It is something they would have received in any event but they would have had to wait longer for it. It is not in the category of a rip-off. The same kind of tax treatment is given to developers in the United States.
By the way, Mr. Chairman, clause 6 ensures that carrying charges on land held by speculators do not get similar treat-
Income Tax Act
ment. It is only on land held by a land developer, somebody who is developing land, that gets this treatment.

Mr. Chairman, because the so-called developers are taking their money, going to California and investing it in other countries where they can make big bucks,
I do not see how the minister can stand up and tell this House that by giving this $30 million away to these developers it will put low income Canadians into housing. The problem is not the fact that they are going to build a house, it is whether people can afford to pay for the bloody homes. That is the problem. 1 know this is lifting mortgage interest deductibility to new heights; it is a mortgage interest deductibility for developers. It seems to me this is one way that they can write off the cost of the money borrowed to buy the land under the guise of developing it. As far as I am concerned I do not see how that will be helpful to Canadians.
The minister said that he feels somehow morally committed to this particular budget brought in by his predecessors, and we must all keep in mind that the minister is a recycled Liberal so it should not be difficult for him to make this quantum leap of credibility. Can he tell us that if he drops that particular clause, for example, that somehow or other we will not get housing for Canadian people? I do not think he should go along with a rip-off scheme that his buddies in the Liberal party designed for their corporate friends. I think he should come clean with the Canadian people on that one.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman speaks with his usual moderation, and I note his comments. However,
1 do not believe the hon. gentleman understands the situation. If you are a real estate developer, the money does not just leap into your hands. You have to take risks, you have to invest, you have to put your money out, you have to pay interest on the money borrowed, and property and municipal taxes have to be paid. These are costs to you in your development.
If this clause is not passed the situation is this; these costs can generally only be deducted when you have made a sale of the land, that is, when you have developed it and divided it up and sold it. These costs interfere with cash flow and you can only recover them when the land is sold. This provision simply provides that you can deduct these currently. In other words, you do not have to wait until the land is sold to deduct them. You can deduct them earlier than that. All you are doing is deducting something that you had to wait a longer time to deduct. This enables you to sell your land cheaper and to sell lots for less.
It is not any rip-off. There is no crime involved. The real estate developers of this country are not all criminals, frauds or crooks-there might be one or two who are not 100 per cent, as there are in every group, but I do not see why they should be attacked as rip-off artists and all the rest just because there is a suggestion that provision should be made to help them to improve their cash flow position in order to lower the cost of developed land.

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, nobody said that they were doing anything illegally. It is fairly obvious that this is legalized pickpocketing.
Since the minister said all of these things, which he has described in this particular clause, have resulted in these people developing land and turning it back to people at reasonable costs, has his department done any study to see if that is happening, that land is coming into production in terms of house building at reasonable costs? All indications are that they have gone out of sight. For example, in the municipality of Toronto you cannot get a house under $70,000. Even in an area like my own, you do not touch a home for under $55,000. How can a person making $13,000 a year afford to own a home in Canada? Yet, we find that that is still one of the great incentives in this country of ours, that home ownership is still very attractive to Canadians. If that is not doing what it is supposed to do, then all we are doing is allowing legalized pickpocketing of Canadian taxpayers as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, as far as I know the Department of Finance has done no additional studies on this. A study was done by a federal-provincial task force headed by Mr. Greenspan, a Toronto lawyer who is very familiar with the real estate business. He studied this question, and it is his recommendation. So the hon. gentleman can relax. Everything is all right. There was a royal commission study and a report made. I do not think he needs to worry himself any more about it. Let us get this provision passed so the hon. gentleman will not have indigestion.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister has said it there is nothing like getting Mr. Greenspan, a man who is a friend of the developers, to do the study. It is like giving the Avon route here in Kanata to the son of Sam. It seems to me that is exactly the kind of thing that concerns us on this side of the House. Since developers have been operating under this particular clause, has the minister studied the effect this clause has had on the housing market? In effect, is it doing the things that Mr. Greenspan said it would do for his friends?
Mr. Chairman, we have done no studies. If the House passes this provision then we will certainly be keeping an eye on it to see whether it is effective or not, and what the results of it are.

Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of questions for the minister. It is interesting to note that the minister is taking his advice from Liberal economists who are friends of the real estate industry.
I spoke earlier about the question of tax expenditures. Can the minister tell this House whether he feels the $30 million which this program will be costing the people of Canada is best spent in this assistance to land developers, or does he think that perhaps the $30 million would not be better spent, for example, in making retroactive the provisions for spouse's allowance, for assisting the fishermen of Newfoundland, or perhaps assisting in defraying the costs of urban rapid transit?
I ask the minister to confirm to this House that it is his view

that this assistance to developers takes a higher priority than that particular aid?

Mr. Chairman, that has all the appearance of a loaded question to me. I think there are many, many thousands of demands upon the revenue of Canada. If I had my way 1 would like to see billions upon billions spent on the needs and requirements of the fishermen of Newfoundland. If I had no one else to bother me, that is where all the money would be going. We would be putting it right into Newfoundland and forgetting the rest of the country. The first priority would be St. John's West; second, the province of Newfoundland, and after that the rest of you. That is, if I did not have to consider anything else and if I could only consider the real priority. But there are thousands of other priorities. One is metropolitan areas, and land development in metropolitan areas, urban areas, and land development across the country.
All the industries we have in this country have to be considered along with the co-operatives, the credit societies and the unions. The whole mosaic has to be considered in our taxation system. In a budget of $52,600 million-and there would be a lot more if we included the tax expenditures but I do not have the figure ready tonight-we would have to add on another $8 billion to $10 billion in tax expenditures. As a result of this particular provision, $25 million to $30 million is the amount by which federal revenues would be reduced in 1979-80. That revenue would have been lost eventually under the present system. This is only to help improve the cash flow of the land developer.
Whenever you ask should "X" have priority over "Y", I can think of a lot of "Y's" that I would like to see have priority over this, but it is a balanced taxed system and it has to be a balanced government. There are a whole lot of provisions in this tax act, and you can ask me the same questions, but everytime I will tell you I think it should be spent on the fishermen, that this would have top priority for them. However, my views cannot carry the day. We have to have a balanced system.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister please indicate again, and I will ask the question again because it was not answered, whether he is prepared to agree that instead of giving $30 million to assist land developers, he is prepared to put this money into programs that would make the spouse's allowance retroactive?

Mr. Chairman, I thought I had just answered the question. If I have not answered the question, I apologize to the hon. gentleman. But no, I do not think it should go into retroactive payments of the spouse's allowance. I do not think it should go into retroactive payments of salaries for members of this House, or into doubling of salaries. I do not think it should go into anything else. I think it should be exactly where it is in this bill and, if we pass it, this revised treatment will reduce our revenues. We are not spending the money. It will reduce the revenues we take in by $25 million to $30 million in an attempt to help the development of land throughout Canada. Therefore, lots will cost less and developers will be
October 30, 1979

encouraged. They will get the same treatment as in the United States, and we will carry out the recommendations of a royal commission report.

One final question, Mr. Chairman. This question was asked previously in another fashion. Can the minister tell us what evidence, if any, he has that this money which is being forgone, the $30 million, will produce the effect he says it will produce? What evidence does the minister have for that?
Only time will tell.
Is the minister prepared to answer the question?
Mr. Chairman, only time will tell.
Mr. Chairman, I think there is a legitimate philosophical difference of opinion between the minister and this party.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We agree.

I hear from the intelligentsia on the other side that 1 am right. That difference is very important.
In the development industry, the picture in the minds of members opposite is obviously of a highly competitive industry which needs to be assisted in terms of cash flow, and recommends the assistance of the government and taxpayers of Canada. It is very clear from studies commissioned by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation that the facts are quite the reverse. The question is very' fundamental-whether we give $60 million to Ford to set up a factory in Windsor, whether we give substantial sums of money in super depletion allowances to the oil industry, or whether we give speedy, exaggerated depreciation of capital cost allowances such as we are doing in the development industry.
There is a very legitimate difference of opinion on this side of the House. We say this is a very lousy way to spend public money. If we are to have a free enterprise system, let's put a little freedom back into it. Let's get you free enterprisers out of the public trough. Let's see the freedom put back in the system. Let's see that initiative and urge to provide for the competitive system.
We do not see that. We see a highly concentrated, highly oligopolistic system with a few large companies controlling more and more, whether it be land, automobiles, oil or whatever. We see those same companies coming back to the government saying, "Give us another handout, another favour, another $30 million, another $60 million, another speed-up of our depreciation.'' They want to wipe out their costs in two years. They do not want to pay more taxes.
We are hammering this. The minister can shake his head and others can say this is ideological clap-trap. We are not
Income Tax Act
being ideological. We are looking at this increasing concentration in our society and looking at these large economic units, whether or not they have a personality, as the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount, who gave us a learned discourse on corporate personality this afternoon, said. I do not care if they have a personality or not. All I know is that our tax system is being pillaged by these people.
This is a legitimate question which we will raise in this and other instances. We will insist that it be brought to the attention of the people. We will not allow the bill to go through without it being brought to their attention. If we believe in freedom of information, some of this information should come out. The Canadian people should decide whether we want to have doctors and lawyers putting money into development and not paying taxes. That is a very important question.
We want to have information on the development industry, how it works and where it goes. We are perfectly entitled to have that. With great respect to the minister, we have a different point of view. Our point of view is that it is increasingly senseless for the tax system of this country to be used to subsidize those people who should be able to stand on their own two feet. I used to think there were people in the Conservative party who had that same view, but they do not seem to be around any more. The doctrine of corporate welfare seems to have taken over from the doctrine of free enterprise.

Mr. Chairman, 1 see nothing wrong with the hon. member having his point of view, or his party having a point of view. This is good. Let us get it on the record. You are against the real estate developers being given any kind of break at all in order to lower the costs of their land. You are against them being allowed to deduct their costs in the year they incur them. They have interest costs. They pay taxes. Why should they not be allowed to deduct those costs in the year in which they incur them? It would help their cash flow. They would be able to buy raw land, develop that land and bring lots on to the market. 1 understand you are against that.
I am in favour of you bringing out these points so that we and everyone else will know where we are opposed and where we disagree. I congratulate you for doing that. I understand your position exactly. In this case you are not correct, but it is a legitimate difference.

For the edification of the minister, and for clarification as far as this party is concerned, we are not ignorant of the fact that land costs need to be lowered. What we are concerned about is that despite the gifts out of the public treasury to a fat cat group of developers, we have seen no evidence that the cost of land has been lowered over the years as a result of this.
Large developers control most of the land around our major cities. Viable farmland is constantly being threatened. These are among the most profitable corporations in our country, so profitable that they have money to invest outside our country, yet this government and the members of the official opposition are constantly rushing around in almost feverish disarray to

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
give them more tax benefits. That is what we find unacceptable.
We are not against lowering the cost of land. The minister has already admitted he has no evidence, although he claims this might bring down the cost of land.
I see the government whip. Ele is making all kinds of rude, obscene gestures as he waddles his way back and forth behind the curtains. Has he ever stood up in this place and made one knowledgeable comment? Not since I have been here, and 1 have been here as long as he.
What we are concerned about is not whether the government gives the real estate industry some $30 million as a gift for past favours or whatever, but does it or does it not lower the cost of land in this country? Will the purchaser of land receive a direct benefit from this? If the minister can assure us of that, we will be very pleased to vote for this clause.

In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the man or woman who purchases the land will have a benefit from this. It is not just for the developer. It will help development and those who buy lots. That is our opinion. We will have to wait and see if it has that effect.

Mr. Chairman, I find it interesting that the minister continues to tell us the developers need this extra benefit or incentive in order to operate; that they need to improve their cash flow. We are told they are paying their fair share of taxes.
After we started discussion on this clause, I walked over to the Parliamentary Library to get a book which 1 would recommend to the minister, entitled "The Developers", by James Lorimer. I want to put on record some of the facts this author obtained from public records that are available. Let me refer to some paragraphs in this book. Mr. Lorimer said, and I quote:
-developers who own income properties are able to avoid paying corporate tax on the profits they make in all the various aspects of the land development business.
They do this precisely through the kind of proposal we find in the bill we are discussing. Mr. Lorimer goes on to illustrate what he means in the following way. He says:
Following its own prescription, Daon-
That's one of the big land developers around the city,
declared profits of $21,558,000 in 1977. It paid no corporate tax at all on these profits. Cadillac Fairview declared profits of $31.5 million in 1977 and paid taxes totalling $1.7 million, an effective rate of tax of about 6 per cent. On declared profits of $8.6 million in 1976, Trizec paid a minuscule $130,000 in tax.
He says:
Since it was established, the land development business has benefited from an arrangement that means that most developers do not now and never have paid substantial amounts of corporate tax on their profits. The actual rate of tax paid by the industry over all is much less than 10 per cent, probably 5 to 6 per cent. Most other industries, of course, pay corporate tax on profits in the range of 40 to 50 per cent.

That is precisely the point we are trying to make. Nobody in this party calls the developers criminals, as the minister tried to imply a few moments ago. The developers are doing only what they are permitted to do under the law, and if we have governments which are stupid enough to permit them to pay corporate tax of less than 10 per cent, then, of course, they are going to take advantage of the laws we pass. And going to a lawyer who was appointed by another party when it was in power, going to a lawyer who has intimate connections with the real estate and development industry, seems to me the last place to which a government should turn for advice, not the first place. It is like inviting a fox into a chicken coop and asking him to protect the chickens.
Mr. Lorimer goes on to give a few more illustrations. I should like to put part of what he says on record.
Daon is one developer that reports both its operating profit and its appraisal surplus profit every year. In 1973, Daon reported that it had accumulated appraisal surplus profits totalling $17 million. In 1974, the figure was $21 million, up $4 million in the year. By 1976, the amount was $55 to $60 million, an appraisal surplus profit of about $35 million in two years. In 1977 it was $126 million meaning an appraisal surplus profit of an amazing $66 million that year. Daon's operating profit in 1977, for comparison, was $21.5 million.
The same would be true of Trizec and Genstar and all the other financial wizards who have entered the housing development market and who are making their profit, taking it out of the hide of the ordinary citizen who is trying very hard to do the things he is told every day on the radio, on television and in the newspapers, that he should do-buy a decent, comfortable house for himself and his family.
Keep in mind what the developer does. He goes to the suburbs, he goes to the farmland around a city. I can speak with some personal experience of this, because while Winnipeg has not grown as much as Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary or Edmonton, I know that about a quarter or a third of the people living in houses in my constituency were not there when I was first elected. There were no houses; there were empty fields. There were farmlands there when I was first elected, and that is not so long ago.
Mr. Lorimer calculates that the developer who buys the raw land and puts in the sewers, the water and so on, is making a profit in most cities in Canada of about $20,000 on each lot by the time he sells. Who is paying that money? It is the home purchaser who has to pay-anywhere from $60,000 for a moderately priced home in most Canadian cities to $80,000 or $90,000 or $100,000.
People are putting themselves into debt for their whole lives because of the high cost of housing, and one of the major factors in the high cost of housing in this country is the developer. The developers have done very well, thank you; they have been treated very generously by the people and the governments of Canada. Yet we find the minister coming to this House today and telling us: we have to try to persuade them to do a little more so we are going to give them another tax concession, another $20 million. I say to him that this will not show up in the cost of housing because it has probably been 20 years since there was a year in which a house did not
October 30, 1979

cost between 5 per cent and 10 per cent more than it cost in the previous year.
The minister is compounding the mistakes of former ministers. He is following in the footsteps of former governments. We in the New Democratic Party are not surprised, because we have always felt there is no difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives; the minister is merely demonstrating in this clause that we are correct. What he is saying is that we ought to give more concessions to people who have already done very well. We believe there are better ways, more direct ways, of providing housing for people at prices they can afford than by giving further, and unnecessary, concessions to developers.

The hon. gentleman cited as his authority Mr. Lorimer. I seem to have heard his name before; I think he belongs in the pantheon of NDP saints and it is therefore no more apt for him to call on Mr. Lorimer as his authority than it would be for me or the former minister of finance to call on Mr. Greenspan-it is one man's opinions against another's, it is one study against another. All 1 can say to the hon. member is that he has made the point he wants to make well, but we just don't happen to agree with him.

I do not want to prolong this debate, but 1 say to the minister that he and 1 may, of course, disagree as to the conclusion we draw from factual material-the hon. gentleman will undoubtedly disagree with Mr. Lorimer about what we ought to do. But the figures 1 quoted from Mr. Lorimer's book were obtained from official records of the companies concerned, annual reports which the companies publish showing the profits they make, the taxes they paid, the surpluses, the undistributed reserves, and so on.
If the minister wants to disagree with Mr. Lorimer or with the conclusions we draw, that is quite legitimate, but I do not think he should suggest that the figures 1 have cited are not based on the facts. The figures I used and which I cited from Mr. Lorimer's book are based on the records the companies have made public.

Mr. Chairman, from what 1 have heard so far, I understand that the minister does not like to hear from experts, whether they be Liberal or people who support my party. Perhaps I can give the minister a concrete example of how he can do something to help lower the cost of housing. Maybe I can use an example in the city of Thompson. The minister should know that city well because in April of 1978 he went there and gave a good nominating speech for the incumbent Conservative candidate. Over at Government House the other night 1 thanked the minister for that speech because I think it gave me at least 3,000 votes.
Was that the pussycat speech?

That was the pussycat speech, a very famous speech.
Income Tax Act
Since the minister knows the city of Thompson so well, he should also know that there is land banking in that city. We have had it ever since the city became a city. As a result, two years ago, in the face of all the cost of developing a lot in the north we were in a position to sell our lots for $8,700. Try to do that in other cities. Try to do it where the government is giving developers all this money. It cannot be done.
Do not bring in Liberal policies. Do not bring in policies which are just as bad as Liberal policies. Bring in something new, something which has been tried in such places as Thompson. Do something for the people of this country. Do not give us a bunch of boloney. 1 would not use the words of the hon. member for Nickel Belt. Give us the truth, something we can really use to lower the price of houses.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has pointed out that the provision we are now discussing is in this bill to permit the deduction of interest and property taxes on land held for development or resale by taxpayers in the ordinary course of their business. 1 would be interested in knowing just how much these interest expenses will be increasing in the next year because of the higher interest rates which have come into effect since the Conservative government took office and, as a result, what the additional revenues lost to the federal government will be because of the higher deductions which will be claimed by developers because of these higher interest costs.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman would ask the hon. member for Saint-Maurice what those figures were when he was minister of finance and when he was originating this bill-and interest rates went up 3.25 per cent during 1978-I dare say he would find that the figures would come out about the same because interest rates have gone up 3.25 per cent in 1979 just as they went up in 1978 when the hon. gentleman was in my position. 1 think the hon. member should be able to get that information quite easily.
With respect to the suggestion of the hon. member for Churchill, the purpose of this change, which was recommended by the Greenspan task force and which caused this change in the law making the law as it was before, was to help the small developer. This is a provision which is to help small developers in Canada, not large developers. Large developers do not need any help. They already have ample cash flow. They can already do very well. This is a provision to help hundreds and hundreds of small developers in Canada get the cash flow necessary to carry on their businesses. If hon. gentlemen are against the small developer, they should vote against this provision.
If hon. gentlemen are against this provision, let us have a vote on the matter and settle it one way or the other. We believe it is necessary and legitimate and that it will help the small developers of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, is the minister telling us that he does not have figures he can give us at this time regarding the revenue lost to the government which will be created by the increase in interest rates since his government took office? It is

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
not enough to tell us what happened before the election. Let us hear what has happened since the minister took office. That is what we have to talk about now.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have the figure. How could I possibly know how much real estate development there will be this year, how much activity there is going to be, what loans are going to be like, what property taxes they have to pay, or how much they are going to have to pay in interest? If interest rates have gone up, and we know they have, presumably their interest costs will be a bit higher, and the figure here might not be $25 million to $30 million. It might be a bit more; I have no way of knowing.
I am not a fortune teller, so 1 cannot answer that question, as the hon. member knows. He thinks he is making some clever point about interest rates. He knows that interest rates have gone up because we have no reasonable alternative. He has not been able to suggest a reasonable alternative, so what is the point of his question? The point of his question is that the hon. gentleman thinks it is smart. Well, fine. If he thinks it is smart, he has made his point.

Mr. Chairman, there is a reasonable alternative. It is the one which was presented by his leader on March 2 when he spoke as leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. He said that a Progressive Conservative government would bring interest rates down. I suggest that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister ought to get together. I think they are both in the inner cabinet; or have we missed something? Is the Minister of Finance no longer in the inner cabinet? Surely the officials in the department at the time this budget was presented made some forecasts of the revenue effects. It is my understanding that they do that with respect to all proposals in a budget. Surely it is possible to update those forecasts. Can the minister not give us the information?

Mr. Chairman, the estimate which was prepared by the department is that it might cost $25 million to $30 million, and I think that is still a good estimate, despite the increases in interest rates. So, I stick by the estimate, $25 million to $30 million.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to note that while the minister wishes to stick by that estimate, 1 am sure that some elementary calculation by his officials will show that the revenue lost to the Canadian taxpayer will go up substantially because of the interest rate increases which have gone into effect since the minister became Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, first I must comment on the arrogance of the Minister of Finance. 1 know that that was the favourite tune hon. members opposite sang when they were in opposition. They sang about the arrogance of the government across the way at that time, yet I find the minister's attitude arrogant and disinterested. He asks us to get on with it, pass the thing and "Let's go". He tells us not to enter into any meaningful discussion about the implications of this $30 million handout. 1 think that is very important to keep in mind.

When the Minister of Finance sat on the opposition benches and as he, the happy hacker, and a few others, were official critics of the finance portfolio, they all condemned this budget when it was presented. They even introduced motions of non-confidence. Now the minister is responsible for the finances of this country, and he starts off by saying he wants to be known as Mr. Tough Guy and no more Mr. Nice Guy. This is his first chance to be the Mr. Tough Guy who is concerned about the shekels of this country. Why does he not say to his corporate friends in the development world that they cannot have this $30 million and that it is not in Canada's best interests at the moment? We have a stagnant housing market because of interest rates. Therefore, in effect, we should not be giving the minister's corporate friends something we cannot afford at this time. When the minister gets tough with little people, he has some credibility.
I want to call a spade a spade. We know well that the real estate developers in the city of Toronto wasted considerable amounts of money for the Tory campaign in the last federal election. In effect, that is where that interest lies.
It is not that the minister thinks that for eight months the government went on the old budget and he feels morally committed to continue it. Good heavens, the Conservatives waged a whole campaign against unemployment insurance changes. They were down in eastern Canada arguing against the Liberal government's changes in Bill C-14. When they came to power, the first thing the Conservatives did was to allow the changes to go into effect. How can that be called credibility? How can we say that the Canadian people should not look at this House of Commons as a pile of hypocrisy? The minister has the reins of power in his hands. He can be Mr. Tough Guy with Trizec. The minister says this is for little developers. How can we separate the little developers from the big developers?
With a crowbar.
My colleague, the hon. member for Broad-view-Greenwood, says, "With a crowbar".
You can't pry them apart.

In effect we are getting a concentration of developable land in few hands, and in many parts of this country there is no legislation to protect farmland. There are no laws to ensure that farmland is protected. That is a very important problem, and 1 challenge the Minister of Finance to show how tough he is. There is more than just this $30 million. There is a whole pile of giveaways in this bill which we will be dealing with in Committee of the Whole tonight. I want the minister to live up to the image of Mr. Tough Guy he has cast for himself. I want to see him go to town on these particular giveaways in this budget.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance indicated that the benefits of this tax concession for developers would go to small developers. I wonder if he is aware of the fact that most of the major oil companies, with the tremendous revenues
October 30, 1979

they have been generating this year in the United States and Canada, are going into housing developments, and whether he has taken that into consideration. Proposals have already been made by the Conservative energy caucus, by the Canadian Petroleum Association, and last evening by the Premier of Alberta, that they want to move energy prices up dramatically. The Premier of Alberta suggested that they go right to world prices this next year.
In the United States, with the rapid increase in energy prices, the oil companies have shown profits of up to 211 per cent over the same quarter in the last year. This is building up as the rapid increase takes place. Is any other consideration being given to the fact that large amounts of these petro revenues will be syphoned off into urban and land development and whether it is really in the best interests of the country to be giving special concessions to oil companies which are generating these huge revenues?
In the third quarter of this year we see that the profits of oil companies have gone up from 38 per cent to 66 per cent for four of the majors. All the argumentation that has been brought forth regarding increased oil revenues is that it is going to be ploughed back into the high Arctic and the frontier areas, and it seems to me that if that is not going to take place we can hardly justify the massive increases in the price of crude oil and products from the refining processes.
I wonder if the minister has taken that into account in putting before the House tonight this special concession for land development, whether an excess profit tax will be brought in if the government goes ahead with the massive increase in the oil price of $3, $4, $7 or $8, as has been suggested by his caucus and by the Premier of Alberta. Can the minister tell us just what has been taken into account in that regard?

It is the first time I have heard any suggestion that oil moneys are behind this clause in the bill. This clause originated in the budget of November 16, 1978, which was brought by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. Whether he had in mind the oil industry at the time he brought it in, whether he had it in mind that oil money was going to go into the real estate development market, I do not know. It has not crossed my mind for one minute that this was a sinister plot for the oil industry to get some tax concessions. I certainly never imagined that.
What it is is that real estate developers up to now were only allowed to deduct the cost of interest on their loans and the cost of property taxes when they had sold the land in question. When they have sold the land in question, they are allowed to deduct these as costs. They have to carry it the rest of the time, so it is an added burden on them. Small real estate developers, as was found by the Greenspan inquiry, had to carry that burden, which interfered with their cash flow. Their business is developing lands and lots for sale, and therefore interest and municipal taxes are a legitimate expense of that business. This clause proposes that those taxes and interest expenses be recognized as ordinary expenses and that they be
Income Tax Act
allowed to deduct them on an annual basis, which would help their cash flow position.
Clause 66 in the bill ensures that the current charges held by speculators be maintained and that they do not benefit from that kind of treatment. If you just bought some land hoping it will go up in value and if you hold on to it for a few years, you will not get this treatment. But if you are in the business of developing real estate, it is legitimate. If you are a speculator, you will not get it.
I know of no evidence or suggestion that this will in any way be of help to the oil and gas industries, or that the revenues will have anything to do with them. This provision is to help the small real estate developer improve his cash flow position. If there is a better way of developing real estate, that is fine. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite believe the government should develop it all. They believe in the state doing it. That is an option, but it is not an option we will take. When hon. gentlemen take over, when they get the reins into their hands, the old reins in their paws, they can eliminate the private real estate development industry, do away with it, squash it flat, knock it out, make sure it cannot survive, make sure it has no cash flow, make sure only the state and public agencies have the ability to carry on real estate development. When that time comes, they can do so, but at present for the most part it is in private hands in Canada, and this is a legitimate amendment to help the small real estate developer.
I do not know how much more reasonable I can be about it. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to vote against it, I say, fine, vote against it, and those who want to vote for it, let them vote for it, and those who want to discuss it, let them discuss it. In no way are we trying to force this thing through. We could not do it any way, and therefore it is a dialogue and I am delighted to hear from the hon. gentlemen. I wish I had realized I had the reins in my hand. There are a lot of things I would have done if I had known it then.

Mr. Chairman, there must have been a reason why, as the minister has told us, the situation has now reverted to the way it was before. Can the minister tell us the reason why the situation was changed and now it has to be brought back? Was there some purpose in the earlier change?

1 cannot tell the hon. member, except that the Liberal administration had it one way before and they changed it to another way. Then they introduced a budget reverting back to the original way. My colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, is not here to help me with this bill. Where is he when I need his assistance?
Oh, oh!
It's your baby now.

Has it occurred to the minister that perhaps he is helping more by staying away than by being here?
Obviously we are going to vote against this clause and against clause 6-I do not think it is a secret to the minister- but I want to put the minister on notice that, first of all, we

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
look forward to intensive study by this government as by the previous government, on the question of inflation in land prices. We look forward with eager anticipation to the minister's coming to this House and telling us what the inflationary developments in land have been over the past years, and we look forward with eager anticipation to his confirming his thesis that he is giving assistance to a highly competitive industry and that the immediate impact of these measures will be to reduce the cost of land to the average Canadian consumer, and of course, this will be reflected to lower housing costs which we can also anticipate as a result of the proposals.
Earlier we had spoken about the nature of the development industry and the concentration in the housing industry. The minister is saying that here he is giving something for the smaller developer. That is not what is happening because there is no selectivity here, and this is the problem with the whole tax spending system. There is no selectivity, no direction of tax dollars, no control over whether this provision will have the effect the minister says he wants it to have. It is going to everybody.
I would be willing to place a moral wager with the minister that the result of this measure will be that the amount of concentration in the development industry will be increased and not decreased, as sure as it snows in the wintertime. If the minister thinks he will increase competition in any industry by giving a tax incentive which applies right across the board, he is dreaming. If he did it in the car industry, he would be laughed out of Detroit, Windsor, Oakville and Oshawa. If he is serious about increasing competition in our society, he would not be serving under a Prime Minister who in a May, 1979, interview in Executive magazine said that competition was not a priority of the Conservative government, that competition was being put on the back burner by his government. It was not something which was causing him a great deal of concern.
I do not think competition is something which gives this government concern at all.
The minister is shedding crocodile tears when he talks about giving help to the small developer. He is not being realistic about the structure of the development industry. He is kidding himself and members of his party if he thinks this will do anything for the little person or the little developer in our society. It will not work that way. I think the minister should realize it.

Mr. Chairman, earlier on in reply to a question the minister referred to the fact that for some reason we wanted government ownership of the land. That is what we were talking about when giving an example of how land can be cheaper in northern cities, even without the type of giveaway the minister is presently presenting. I should like to remind the minister that the mayor of Thompson is a Conservative, that the majority of the council is Conservative. He should know. He met them all. Those people do not want to privatize our land. They know what is a good deal. They do not have to sell everything to private ownership. They want to find good,

cheap land for the people of Thompson. I wish the minister had the same concern here.
In reply to a question which I did not ask, the minister said that he was helping small developers by the presentation being made at this time. Does the minister have the facts at his disposal to prove that this is not another giveaway to large corporations? Can he prove that it will not do what the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said? Will it not help to increase the concentration of ownership? Does he know the incomes of the developers who are presently using this giveaway? Does he know what the breakdown is?

Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the minister. He has indicated his concern with the small developer, as he calls him. Can the minister indicate to the committee what proportion of the entire land development industry is made up of what he calls small developers? If the hon. minister is so concerned about small developers and not the big ones, can he indicate whether he is prepared to introduce an amendment to this particular provision so that it will apply only to small developers?

Mr. Chairman, this clause stands by itself. What is correct for one developer is correct for another. The people that this will help most are the small developers, because they have more difficult cash flow problems than the few large developers. As to what the respective numbers are, I would have to make an educated guess. I would say there are many thousands of small real estate developers in Canada and that there are a few dozen large developers. That is my guess. I do not have the statistics here. I did not come supplied with them tonight. 1 do not know whether we could even obtain them. There are many thousands of small developers. The large developers would number in the dozens. The numbers do not matter because we are amending the law for all real estate developers so that they can deduct on an annual basis legitimate business expenses for developing their land.

Mr. Chairman, I have sat here listening with some interest over the past hour or so. A couple of matters popped into my mind. A lot of people in my riding have been without housing for some time. Under neither previous administration or this one, the federal government has not made any distinctive attempt to deal with the housing situation nor with any ongoing income supplements such as unemployment insurance.
Looking back at the comments made by a number of members on the government side and the comments just made by the minister that there are a few thousand developers, why do we not put it in a nutshell so that the Canadian public can understand? Why do we not say that the government is planning to send out cheques to every developer in Canada for $10,000 or $15,000? But the people who need $150 or $160 every two weeks from their unemployment insurance do not get it from the very same government. I think we should deliver the facts to the Canadian public and be quite frank. It is not for small developers. It is not necessarily for big developers. It is for all of them. It is very, very obvious to me
October 30, 1979

that it is patronage. Let us put it in cheque form and mail it from the House today. I think we are quibbling on a clause which should not be passed in a country which is facing economic difficulties.
1 have a couple of questions which have been opened up by the great concern expressed by the minister for the small developer. What does the minister mean by a small developer? How big is small?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister.
The hon. minister is not answering the question.
Was that a question?

Since the hon. minister does not seem to know how big is small when he talks about small developers, aside from the numbers involved-and there may be many thousands-what proportion of the development industry in terms of percentage do these so-called small developers actually hold? 1 know in my own constituency of Burnaby over 80 per cent of the development land is controlled by the five big land development companies. What proportion in terms of percentage do these so-called small developers occupy of the land development market?

How big is small? How small is big? How big is little? How little is big? The hon. member's guess is as good as mine. We could adopt the definition of small business and say that real estate companies are less than the definition of a small business in the Income Tax Act; that that is a small developer. That would probably be suitable.
1 really do not see the rest of the point of the hon. member. If the hon. gentleman has five big developers in Burnaby or wherever it is, and if he does not have any small ones, that is unfortunate. I am sorry. I know down in Newfoundland we have a lot of small developers. We do not have too many big ones. But we are not as big as British Columbia. We are little. Where British Columbia is big, we are little. Where it is great, we are small. What is small? What is great? The small is greater than the big in my opinion in the province of Newfoundland.

Mr. Chairman, the people of Burnaby will be interested to hear that this proposal does nothing for them, but helps the big developers in Burnaby.
I ask the minister whether he is prepared to limit this particular benefit to small developers, however he defines them? Is the minister's answer "No"? The minister says no.
It should be answered for the record.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to get down to specifics with the minister. Can he name a small developer that would go out of existence if he did not get help from this $30 million handout? Can he name one small developer?
Income Tax Act
1 think the minister said that the developer does not have to sell the property, that he does not have to sell the land in order to enjoy the write-off. Can he confirm that? Will he get it before the sale of the land or after the sale of the land?

I cannot name one small developer that will go out of business if this does not pass. No, I am afraid I cannot do that. There are hundreds of people who will get their building lots hopefully at lesser prices if this goes through, because the land developers' costs will be a bit less and the cash flow will be a bit better. I would suspect there would be hundreds, if not thousands, who might be helped to buy lots. Could the hon. member remind me of his second question?
Do they receive the benefit of this concession after the sale of the land?

No, no. That is the purpose of this concession, as the hon. member calls it. The way it works is that these companies are in business. Every year they have their accounts as they have their year endings. Every 12 months they have a financial statement, they have their revenues and their expenses, and each year they have the interest on the inventory of land. They have their tax expenses in relation to that land although they have not sold the land yet, and they would be allowed to deduct that as a present current expense. That is the only difference. Under the present system they can only deduct those kinds of costs as they sell the land out of their inventory. This helps them with the cash flow situation. They would still have this deduction at a point in time. It is just that they get the deduction at an earlier point, as long as they continue to stay in business.
That is the way I understand it to work. Perhaps I am all wrong, but I think that is how it works. All we are doing here would be allowing them to get this deduction earlier than they are now able to get it, unless they are able to turn over their inventory of land every year. Of course, a lot of them are not able to do that and they have it longer than that.

speechtext: Shall clause 2 carry?
Agreed.

No.
Clause 2 agreed to; yeas 35; nays, 12.
Clauses 3 and 4 agreed to.
On clause 5-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood rising on clause 5?
I am standing in respect of clause 5, Mr. Chairman. Could the minister explain this clause?

I will try it once. This section 15 of the act deals with a number of shareholder benefits. This particular amendment affects income bonds and income debentures. It is

October 30, 1979
Income Tax Act
a technical amendment and is not directly related to the major change proposed in the budget in the treatment of those income bonds and term preferred shares dealt with in clause 6. The two subsections that would be affected by this amendment refer to "annual or other periodic amount payable on an income bond". The amendment substitutes the words "interest or dividends" for the expression "annual or other periodic amounts". The change is to clarify the scope of the two subsections. It ensures that only the dividend or the interest and not any repayment of the principal will be treated as a dividend in the hands of the recipient. That is what the change is about.
What does it mean?

That's a good question. It is to ensure that you cannot get repayment of the principal, but that you can only get under this section of the act the dividend or the interest, and the repayment of the principal of an income bond or a term preferred share is not treated as interest or dividend.
I do not want to make a long speech on this subject, Mr. Chairman, but-
But I will.

The hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount gave an interesting speech this afternoon, some of which I agreed with and some of which I disagreed with, and the minister commented on the complexity of the Income Tax Act.
I will be quite blunt with the minister. My concern is that this House sitting as a Committee of the Whole is unable to understand what it is passing. The minister reads out of his brief from his officials. I do not blame him for that. If any one of us on this side were in his chair we would be in exactly the same position, but he is unable to explain to the Canadian taxpayer in simple words the meaning of the changes on which we are all voting. I am not prepared for my part, and I cannot speak for any other member of my party, to accept this package. I am very reluctant to say "ready; aye, ready" to a series of amendments that are extremely complex, which can hardly be understood, and even when we read them with the Income Tax Act are almost impossible to comprehend. Many of us do not understand the instruments that are being described.
The average Canadian does not know what a term preferred bond or an income bond is, and does not have a clue as to what they are or precisely what we are voting on. I am not ashamed to profess ignorance, and I think it would be healthy if all members of this House asked; what the hell is this instrument we are talking about and what are we doing here? I think we all might learn something from this exercise. We are going to end up putting in several pages of amendments to the Income Tax without being able to justify to our constituents what we have been doing. I think we owe it to ourselves to have an explanation as to why we are saying "ready; aye, ready" to a bunch of clauses which have gone through the Department of Finance and which have not been sifted through or homoge-

nized by the Minister of Finance. I think we deserve that process of homogenization by him.

Mr. Chairman, let me try again to homogenize. The amendment is to replace the expression "an annual or other periodic amount" with the expression "an amount paid as dividend". This has been the wording in this clause, in line with other provisions of the act, and it is to ensure that this subsection does not apply to any repayment of the principal amount of the security. It could be argued, for example, that the annual repayment of principal on a sinking fund issue would constitute "an annual or other periodic amount", and would thus qualify as a dividend. In other words, if this wording is not changed there is a possibility of a mistake in interpretation, and when you pay an annual amount on principal on a sinking fund issue that could be taken to mean "annual or other periodic amount", treated as a dividend and received by another corporation exempt from tax in their hands. The note goes on to suggest that as such a repayment would be exempt from tax in the hands of the corporation, and the corporation would have a loss on the disposal of the income debenture, and this result is clearly unintended. This amendment now before the committee is proposed to do away with the possibility that this unintended effect could occur. It is to clarify this. It is a technical amendment to the act which only lawyers could draft, and I doubt that most of them could even understand it.
Clause 5 agreed to.
On clause 6-

Mr. Chairman, 1 want to indicate to the minister that, as I said before, we look forward to the evidence, which was so lacking with the Liberal government and which we consistently looked for, to deal with the problem of concentration in the land and housing industry. We needed a series of clear proposals that would deal with the problem of concentration.
The one point the minister made that I want to respond to, Mr. Chairman, is that somehow we are going to march Canada into some totalitarian future, where all Canadians would wear the same clothes, where there would be no diversity and the state would do everything. That is not the point. The point is that some resources, such as land, might be publicly owned-owned by municipalities, by provinces, by co-operatives, and some might be owned privately. We are the party that wants diversity; we are in favour of diversity. All we are saying is that this determination to give everything to the private sector is a guarantee that there will be concentration and not diversity.
It is precisely because we want diversity in the housing industry, because we want things to be owned by the provinces, by the cities, by co-operatives, by trade union co-operatives, by many many different kinds of groups, that we believe there must be an active public sector-an active government. Merely giving a series of tax benefits to private corporations
October 30, 1979

and private developers does not deal with the problem. It will not lower the price of a single piece of land, and it will not be passed on to the Canadian consumer.
There is no free market that is working in the Adam Smith world which seems to inhabit the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. It does not exist and it is not working.
May 1 call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

subtopic: AIRPORTS-POSSIBLE DEVELOPMENT OF AIRPORT AT PICKERING-EXPANSION OF TORONTO INTERNATIONAL
AIRPORTS-POSSIBLE DEVELOPMENT OF AIRPORT AT PICKERING-EXPANSION OF TORONTO INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 25 I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) arising from the southern Ontario multimodal passenger studies. My question related to the possible expansion of the Toronto International Airport and maintenance of the lands at Pickering. I would like to take this opportunity to expand upon my concerns on this matter and the concerns of my constituents in Mississauga North.
The Minister of Transport gave his assurance "that there will be no decision taken on any airport expansion without full consultation with the municipalities involved." I very much
Adjournment Debate
appreciate this assurance, Mr. Speaker, for it is all that my constituents as neighbours of the airport could reasonably expect. We recognize that the ultimate decision on the future role of the present airport must be based largely on the national and the regional interest. All we say is that we wish to have the opportunity to provide input to the decision-making process because, as neighbours, we must live with the consequences of such decisions.
Hon. members will appreciate that living beside Canada's busiest airport is not an unmitigated blessing. Many of the homes in Malton, Cooksville, and Streetsville were built before the airport was located on its present site in 1937. Many others were built within the present airport affected areas of Peel region and Etobicoke before the airport was declared an international airport in 1954.
Last year the Toronto International Airport experienced over 270,000 flights, on an average of about 740 flights per day. For citizens living directly under the flight paths, the environmental damage, particularly in the summer when people are outdoors and windows are open, is more than a simple inconvenience. The noise, especially when only one runway is used for prolonged periods, because of wind conditions, is hazardous both to conversation and one's nerves.
As well, Mr. Speaker, the airport is subject to restricted use during the period from midnight to 7 a.m. However, many people have noticed that these restrictions are honoured more in the breach than is the observance, with the result that their sleep is disturbed.
The major issue of environmental concern, especially to citizens living north and south of the airport, is the possibility of an additional runway. I am pleased, therefore, that the study finds the existing runway system will likely be adequate through to the late 1980s, subject to certain changes in traffic management, procedural measures, and a constraining of general aviation.
The reason that the prospect of a fourth runway is of such concern to these citizens is that the necessary flight paths would affect the homes of some 80,000 people. Many of these citizens have lived in their homes for twenty years and more on the assumption of a certain degree of neighborhood quietude. The construction of a fourth runway in the foreseeable future would be hazardous to their health, to say nothing of my health, and that of my colleagues, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid).
I think it is generally recognized that the question of a third terminal is a different matter. The decision on terminal capacity, as the study reports, can be deferred for a few months. My concern is that the decision be based on the present structural viability of the facilities as they now exist and not be contingent in any way on any additional runway facilities. We appreciate as well that additional terminal requirements will require internal structural changes in parking facilities, baggage handling, ground transportation, and traffic manage-

October 30, 1979
Adjournment Debate
ment. I do not anticipate any serious objections on any such improvements, again as long as they are integrated into the present runway system of the airport.
We in Mississauga North are the first to recognize the vital importance of a viable airport to our community. The airport provides direct employment to 12,000 of our citizens, and secondary employment to many more thousands. As well, many citizens have chosen to live where they do because of proximity to the airport, and others work for companies that are located in Mississauga because of the location of the airport. The Toronto International Airport is important, therefore, to the economic well-being of Mississauga. We are also conscious of the technological improvements in each generation of aircraft, which have resulted in less noisy aircraft engines. Aircraft design engineers forecast even quieter aircraft in the future. It is against these considerations, Mr. Speaker, which we hope the future decision on the airport will be weighed.
In conclusion, I would like to say a few words about the lands at Pickering. I am delighted that the study recommends maintenance of these lands to protect the long-range option of developing a major airport at Pickering. The justification of the former government for the selection of Pickering is a decision which is now very open to question, when one considers the allegations by Walter Stewart in his book "Paper Juggernaut: Big Government Gone Mad". Nonetheless, the taxpayers now have an investment of over $110 million in the lands at Pickering. It is imperative that the long-range options, which Pickering provides to the Ministry of Transport, not be jeopardized. Whatever is done with the lands over the next several years, whether they be used for agricultural or park purposes, it is important that those options be kept open for the future.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I applaud the preparedness of the Minister of Transport to seek out a suitable vehicle whereby local consultation can take place. We do not need any more studies on our transportation in southern Ontario. The walls of the ministry are white with studies undertaken by the previous government. What we now need is dialogue, consultation, and then decisions to be followed by actions based on the long-term interests of the country, the region and the affected communities.

speakeroldname: Mr. Otto Jelinek (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-POSSIBLE DEVELOPMENT OF AIRPORT AT PICKERING-EXPANSION OF TORONTO INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share some of the concerns expressed by the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Jupp). Let me first provide some background information regarding the discussion paper jointly released by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and the minister of transportation and communications of Ontario.
This paper, called "Southern Ontario Multimodal Passenger Studies", was released to the public on October 15. What I would like to emphasize here is that, first, we have completed a joint study with the province to produce this paper, thus assuring their very valuable participation from the start and

their concurrence with the method used to arrive at decisions in the future. With the province, we have insisted that the paper be released publicly so that all interested parties, whether they be municipal authorities, other government groups, representatives of road, rail or air transportation interests, the academic community, or whatever, be given ample time to review the studies and submit comments. This process has been under way since October 15. I want to be sure everyone interested has had a chance to voice their view, and that this view has been taken into account in the decision-making process.
In this regard, the minister will be announcing in the very near future the make-up of a vehicle which will allow all interested parties, be they municipalities, citizens groups, etc., to be heard and express their views.
This brings me to a very important aspect of the work to date. I am sure we all realize that there are many expenditure options to consider inproviding a passenger transportation system in southern Ontario, including large or small improvements in every mode. It seems to me that we should, as the studies to date suggest, look carefully first at how we can maximize the use of existing facilities to foster fiscal restraint as much as possible, something the previous government ignored, to say the least. We must at the same time keep our eyes on other objectives like conserving energy, encouraging economic development, and protecting the environment. Some of these objectives conflict. However, I am certain that it is wise to retain as much flexibility as possible with respect to the type and timing of transportation expenditures. That is why the Minister of Transport hesitates to throw out any options until full consultation is achieved. The minister wants to be sure every mode of transport is given a fair, effective and efficient role.
I can assure the House and the hon. member that we will not give up any short or long-term option until we, with the province, along with the municipalities and other interested groups, have evaluated the consequences of such a decision and come up with the best course of action.
The Minister of Transport has been assured that no major decision need be taken regarding the Malton facilities or Pickering land for six to 12 months. Within that time we are providing for the public consultation process mentioned earlier, the evaluation of comments, review and updating most recent forecasts of traffic, a closer look at cost of various incremental improvements in corridor rail, bus, STOL, etc.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the various options for the future management of Pickering lands are being analysed and the results of the analysis will form part of the decision-making process.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE-POSSIBLE MOVE OF CANADIAN EMBASSY FROM TEL AVIV TO JERUSALEM-EFFECT ON TRADE
INTERNATIONAL TRADE-POSSIBLE MOVE OF CANADIAN EMBASSY FROM TEL AVIV TO JERUSALEM-EFFECT ON TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I put a question to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) on whether the estimate which had been made recently by some experts as to the amount of trade opportunities which had been lost due to the government s plan to move the Canadian embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem actually amounted to some $5 billion. The minister indicated at that time he was not able to respond precisely to that estimate. I hope he will be able to do so tonight.
He went on in the course of the discussion that day to indicate that there were no studies of a general nature which he could make available to the House-no such studies had been done. I found that strange because that was the day on which we were starting to debate the freedom of information bill and I thought that since it was being introduced he would surely want to make those studies available. If they were not available it seems incredible we would have this situation where billions of dollars worth of trade opportunities were being lost to Canadian businessmen and the department had not carried out studies. I hope the minister will be tabling those studies tonight, knowing full well that eventually we will have the freedom of information bill and that they will be available at that time in any event.
It was interesting that two days later the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin) suggested to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) that perhaps the question of the foreign policy review of the Middle East situation could be separated from the question of the location of the Canadian embassy in Israel. The minister indicated that this could not be done because Mr. Stanfield had to complete his study, he had to travel across the country and engage in further consultations and finally make a recommendation. But yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) did another flip-flop and announced he would be doing exactly what the member for Ottawa-Carleton had recommended, that is, dividing the two questions, with Mr. Stanfield making his report in January on foreign policy review, and the embassy staying in Tel Aviv.
I think we should look back over that sorry four months of confusion and loss of sales to Middle East countries. Back on April 13, 1978, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain as he was at that time, said:
In this country we have companies like Atco which have succeeded in this kind of world market despite the obstacles that governments have put in their way. We would get behind more Canadian companies that have the experience and expertise to serve these markets.
It is incredible how they have got behind Atco, for instance, because they have been sitting with a potential sale to the Middle East worth some $10 million. That deal has been in limbo for the past four months. If that is the way the Prime Minister is getting behind a company, we certainly would not want him to get any closer to them.
Adjournment Debate
It seems to me that what we have to concern ourselves with now is how long term the effects will be. We know that Iraq has an embargo against oil coming into Canada which varies between 15,000 and 30,000 barrels a day. We know that a company in British Columbia, Zenith Steel Fabricators, announced over the weekend that it had lost a $43 million order from one of the Middle East countries. Will those sales be retrieved? We know that Bell had a $3.5 billion order with Erickson and Phillips, and we know that Erickson and Phillips have been asked to extend the contract but Bell has not. All these questions will be answered in the long run, but when we have a government which is facing a $7 billion deficit this year in foreign trade and a suggested $10 billion deficit next year, surely this is a very sorry record for a government which came to power saying it was going to help private enterprise, to help business.
We have a minister of trade who was too late going to the Argentine to get that contract for $1.8 billion for Canadian industry. Now he has to start to try to recoup this estimated loss of $5 billion worth of trade with the Middle East, and we will be very interested and hoping that he will be successful in that, because it means a lot to Canadians in terms of exports, dollars, and jobs.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE-POSSIBLE MOVE OF CANADIAN EMBASSY FROM TEL AVIV TO JERUSALEM-EFFECT ON TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the advice and information the House has been provided by the hon. member. Let me just comment briefly on the trade picture with which we are faced today. This did not happen just over night. This is something which has been developing over a long period of time, and it must be stopped right now. That is one of the reasons this government has identified one person to work solely on the problem of our trade picture.
Let me first get to the specific question the hon. member raised. I said at the time he asked his question, and I say again, that no over-all studies of this particular aspect of the movement of the embassy to Jerusalem have been undertaken. There have been summaries of conversations by me and by officials in the department on the particular experiences of people in the Middle East, of contracts that they are working on and of the relationships we have with Arab clients. These are confidential matters. They are confidential statements. I said that I do not propose to make them public, and I say it again. These are confidential, and if we make these studies public we are not going to receive the benefit of the information these people gain in their work in the Middle East.
1 would like to dispute the statements the hon. member made in connection with lost business. During the course of the period since the early part of June when the statement was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), we have had the summer months. There have been two holiday periods in the Arab countries. As a result, not a lot of business was done over there, so it is fortuitous that this happened at that time, but it is also a fact of life.

October 30, 1979
Adjournment Debate
I might point out that during the course of this period business has been going on. Contracts have been signed. Merchandise exports to Saudi Arabia in August totalled $11.5 million; to Algeria, $15.5 million; to Libya, $2 million; to Egypt, $3.2 million; to Kuwait, $1.1 million; to Iraq, $9.1 million; and so on. So, business is being done and will continue to be done with that part of the world.
I am confident that the businessmen of this country will move quickly to secure the business that they have been negotiating over the past few months.
